trilemma.w: Epistemology needed to say what makes a belief justified. Every proposed answer took the same grammatical form: belief B is justified because of reason R. The trilemma shows that this form of answer can never be completed. It is not a puzzle about some odd class of beliefs — it is a structural fact about the shape of justification itself, which is why it works as the organising problem of the field rather than as one topic within it.
trilemma.i: Push any justification and the chain must do one of three things. It can extend without end, each reason needing a further reason, so that nothing is ever actually established. It can loop, eventually resting on something it was supposed to be supporting. Or it can halt at a proposition you decline to justify further. The three are exhaustive. A chain of reasons is either infinite, closed, or terminated — there is no fourth topology. That exhaustiveness is what gives the argument its force: you cannot escape by being cleverer, only by choosing which failure to live with and then arguing that it is not really a failure.
trilemma.x: Why is this rule justified? Because it reduces harm. Why does reducing harm justify a rule? Because… and now you are on one of the three horns.
trilemma.q: A colleague defends a modelling assumption with “that's just standard in the literature.” Which horn is that, and what is the right follow-up question?
trilemma.a: Horn three — a dogmatic stop with the arbitrariness hidden behind convention. The follow-up: what did the literature's own stop rest on, and has anyone tested whether the result is sensitive to it? Convention does not remove an unjustified assumption; it converts it into an unexamined one, which is worse because nobody now feels responsible for it.

infin.w: The regress problem seems to force a choice between circularity and an arbitrary stopping point. Infinitism exists to show that the first horn—an endless regress—need not be a defect. If reasons can remain available without ever reaching a final foundation, foundationalism loses its claim to be the only way to avoid arbitrariness.
infin.i: Take the first horn and refuse to be embarrassed by it. Infinitism holds that an endless chain of reasons is not a defect. Justification comes in degrees, and each further reason in the chain adds a little more of it. The position is a minority one but it does useful work: it blocks the reflex of treating the regress as obviously fatal and rushing straight into foundationalism. If the regress is survivable, then the argument for foundations has to be made rather than assumed.
infin.x: There is always a further reason available, even if no finite person ever states them all.
infin.q: You ask for a reason, then a reason for that reason, and your colleague says there is always another independently available reason but no final premise. Which response to the trilemma is this, and what must it avoid?
infin.a: Infinitism. It accepts the regress horn but must keep the chain non-circular and explain how finite agents can be justified by reasons they do not all consciously possess at once.

coher.w: If linear chains either regress forever or stop arbitrarily, one response is to reject the chain picture. Coherentism treats justification as a property of a system: consistency, explanatory integration, and mutual support can make the whole web more credible even though no single belief sits outside the web as its foundation.
coher.i: Take the second horn, but widen the circle until it stops looking like a circle. Coherentism denies that beliefs form a chain resting on a base at all. They form a web, and what justifies any strand is how well the whole structure hangs together — its consistency, its mutual support, its explanatory fit. Neurath's image is the standard one: we are sailors who must rebuild the ship plank by plank while at sea, never able to put it in dry dock and start from bare timber. There is no outside vantage point, only the ongoing work of making the structure hold.
coher.x: No single study in a mature empirical literature is foundational. The credibility lives in how the results fit each other.
coher.q: Five studies point the same way, but all use the same database, same coding rule, and same identification assumption. Does coherentism automatically give you five strands of support?
coher.a: No. The web is strong only if the strands supply genuinely different support. Shared dependencies can make apparent coherence one assumption echoed five times; the independence structure matters.

found.w: Foundationalism takes the trilemma’s stopping horn and tries to make the stop principled rather than dogmatic. If some beliefs have immediate justification—through experience, introspection, or another basic status—then inferential beliefs can rest on them without regress or circularity.
found.i: Take the third horn, and argue that the stop is not arbitrary. Foundationalism divides beliefs into a foundation and a superstructure. Foundational — or properly basic — beliefs are justified without resting on any further belief; everything else is justified by its relation to them. The whole dispute then moves to one question: what qualifies a belief as basic? Classical answers appeal to some epistemic privilege — the belief is infallible, indubitable, or incorrigible. Modern answers are more modest, allowing perceptual experience itself to justify a belief about the world without a further belief intervening.
found.x: “I am in pain” does not rest on any further belief. You do not infer it; you are simply in a position to assert it.
found.q: You see a red light and form the belief “the light is red” without inferring it from another belief. What makes this foundationalist rather than merely dogmatic?
found.a: The claim is that the perceptual experience itself supplies prima facie justification. You stop because the justificatory relation is non-inferential at that point, not because you refuse to answer “why?”

hinge.w: Scepticism and the regress problem both assume every meaningful commitment is up for ordinary evidential assessment. Hinge epistemology challenges that assumption. Inquiry needs a relatively fixed background—such as the existence of an external world or the general reliability of memory—against which particular doubts can have sense.
hinge.i: Refuse the framing rather than pick a horn. Wittgenstein's late notebooks argue that some propositions are neither justified nor unjustified. They are the hinges on which the door of inquiry turns — the things that must stay fixed for doubting and checking to be possible at all. Asking what justifies a hinge is a kind of grammatical mistake, like asking what justifies your headache. The hinge is not a very well-supported claim; it is not in the support business. Duncan Pritchard has developed this into a systematic response to scepticism, and it applies to secular bedrock commitments as much as to religious ones.
hinge.x: “The world existed before I was born.” You cannot produce evidence for it without already relying on it.
hinge.q: Someone says, “Prove that the external world existed five minutes ago before you use any memory as evidence.” What would a hinge epistemologist say is wrong with the demand?
hinge.a: The demand asks memory to be validated from a standpoint that already presupposes some framework for evidence and temporal continuity. The relevant commitment functions as a hinge of the practice, not as one more hypothesis inside it.

critrat.w: Critical rationalism takes the trilemma as an argument against the whole project of positive justification. If every attempted justification ends in regress, circularity, or an arbitrary stop, replace justification with criticism. Knowledge can improve by eliminating error even if no theory is ever positively established.
critrat.i: The other refusal. Albert's conclusion from the trilemma is not that we should pick the least bad horn but that the demand for justification was misconceived from the start. Give it up entirely. What replaces it is criticism. You can never show that a theory is supported; you can only expose it to serious attempts to break it and observe that it has not broken yet. Knowledge grows not by accumulating proof but by eliminating error. This is the connection most syllabi miss: the trilemma is the argument for falsifiability. Albert built it as a weapon for Popper's programme, not as a curiosity in the theory of justification.
critrat.x: No number of white swans justifies “all swans are white”. A single black swan settles it. The asymmetry is the whole method.
critrat.q: After two models survive the same tests, one has also survived several risky tests designed specifically to expose its weaknesses. What licenses preferring it on a critical-rationalist view?
critrat.a: Its superior critical record, not a claim that the tests verified or made it probably true. The preference is provisional and comparative: it has withstood stronger attempted refutations so far.

criterion.w: Validation procedures often hide a prior decision about what counts as a successful case. The problem of the criterion exposes that circularity. Particularism begins with cases treated as known and infers standards from them; methodism begins with a standard and lets it classify cases. Neither starting point can be certified without borrowing from the other side.
criterion.i: A sibling of the trilemma, and in some ways sharper. To identify which of your beliefs count as knowledge, you need a criterion. To validate a criterion, you need some cases you already know to be knowledge. Each requires the other first. Chisholm named the two escapes. Particularism starts from confident particular cases and derives the criterion from them. Methodism starts from a criterion and lets it decide the cases. Neither can justify its own starting point.
criterion.x: How do you know the thermometer is accurate? Compare it against a known temperature. How do you know that temperature? You measured it.
criterion.q: You validate a risk score against labels produced by the same expert process the score was trained to imitate. What problem should immediately occur to you?
criterion.a: The problem of the criterion: the benchmark and the method may be validating one another. You need an independently warranted anchor or an explicit admission that one side is being treated as the fixed point.

know.w: True belief is not enough: guesses can be true. Justification seemed to supply the missing ingredient until Gettier showed that a justified true belief can still be true by accident. The contemporary problem is therefore to explain the anti-luck, reliability, competence, or modal connection knowledge adds.
know.i: The analysis question. What must be true for “S knows that p” to be correct rather than merely lucky? For roughly two and a half thousand years the answer looked stable, and then it collapsed in three pages in 1963. What makes this more than a parlour puzzle is the luck condition. We want a notion of knowing that excludes accidentally being right, because only the non-accidental kind is repeatable. A method that happens to produce the correct answer this time is worth nothing next time.
know.x: A stopped clock reads 3:00. At exactly 3:00 you glance at it and believe it is 3:00. Your belief is true. Almost nobody wants to call it knowledge.
know.q: A forecast is correct because two model errors accidentally cancel. Which part of the knowledge problem is this closest to?
know.a: The anti-luck/Gettier problem: the outcome is right, perhaps produced by a respectable process, but the connection between the grounds and the truth is accidental and not robust.

jtb.w: JTB gives a clean decomposition of knowledge into three intuitive requirements: you must believe the proposition, it must be true, and you must have adequate grounds. Its importance now is less that philosophers accept it as sufficient than that almost every later theory can be read as explaining what JTB leaves out.
jtb.i: The classical analysis, and still the working assumption almost everywhere outside philosophy. You know that p if and only if three conditions hold together: p is true, you believe p, and your belief is justified. Each condition earns its place. Falsehoods cannot be known, so truth is required. You cannot know something you do not believe, so belief is required. And a lucky true belief is not knowledge, so a third element is needed to rule out luck. Justification was the traditional candidate for that job.
jtb.x: You believe it is raining; it is raining; and you believe it because you can see it out of the window. All three conditions met.
jtb.q: A person has a justified belief based on a normally reliable source; the belief is true, but only because an unrelated coincidence made the source accidentally right. Which JTB condition fails?
jtb.a: None. That is exactly the Gettier problem: belief, truth, and justification are all present, but the connection between justification and truth is lucky, so JTB is not sufficient.

gettier.w: For over two millennia the analysis of knowledge as justified true belief looked secure. It was not really argued for; it was assumed as the obvious starting point. Gettier's three-page paper showed the three conditions are not jointly sufficient, and in doing so created the research programme that has occupied analytic epistemology ever since.
gettier.i: The recipe is simple once you see it. Take a belief that is justified but false. Derive from it something that is, by luck, true. The derived belief inherits the justification and gains truth — but the justification is tracking the false premise, not the true conclusion. The barn facade variant sharpens it without any false premise. You drive through a county where all but one barn-shaped structure is a film-set facade. You happen to look at the genuine one and believe 'that's a barn'. Your eyesight is fine, your belief is true, and had you looked fifty metres earlier you would have believed the same thing and been wrong. What the cases isolate is epistemic luck.
gettier.x: Your colleague's estimate is correct, and their method was reasonable — but it was reasonable for a different dataset, and it landed on the right answer by coincidence.
gettier.q: A model produced the right forecast last quarter because two specification errors happened to cancel. Is that a Gettier case, and what should you do about it?
gettier.a: Structurally yes: the output is true, the process was defensible on its face, and the connection between them was accidental. The practical consequence is the important part — the result should not raise your confidence in the model at all, because the mechanism that produced it will not reliably reproduce. This is why Gettier matters outside philosophy: it is the argument for auditing process even when outcomes look good, and especially then.

nofalse.w: The original Gettier cases manufacture luck by starting with a justified false belief and validly deriving a true conclusion. The natural repair is therefore to ban false steps in the justificatory route. The proposal matters because its failure reveals that Gettier luck is deeper than simply reasoning from a false premise.
nofalse.i: The first repair attempt: add a fourth condition requiring that the belief not depend on any false intermediate premise. In many Gettier cases the reasoning does pass through something false on its way to something true.
nofalse.q: You identify a real barn in a county full of fake barn facades. Your visual belief uses no false premise. Why does no-false-lemmas still fail to deliver knowledge?
nofalse.a: Because the luck is environmental, not inferential. You could easily have looked at a facade and formed the same belief. The actual reasoning contains no false lemma, yet the belief remains accidentally true.

sens.w: Gettier cases suggest knowledge requires a counterfactual connection between belief and truth. Sensitivity captures the intuition that a knowing method should change its verdict when reality changes: in the nearest worlds where p is false, the subject should not continue believing p.
sens.i: Nozick's condition: you know p only if, had p been false, you would not have believed it. Belief must track truth across nearby possible situations, not merely coincide with it in this one.
sens.x: You do not know the car is in the lot if you would have believed it either way without checking.
sens.q: A stopped clock happens to read 3:00 when it is 3:00. If it were 3:01, you would still believe it was 3:00. What does sensitivity say?
sens.a: The belief is insensitive: in the nearby world where “it is 3:00” is false, the same method still produces the belief. That failure captures why the true belief looks lucky rather than knowledgeable.

safe.w: Safety is a modal anti-luck condition designed to keep what is attractive in truth-tracking while avoiding sensitivity’s rejection of closure. Instead of asking what you would believe if p were false, it asks whether nearby situations in which you form the belief similarly are mostly situations in which the belief remains true.
safe.i: The weaker and more robust cousin of sensitivity: you know p only if you could not easily have believed p falsely. It asks how near the error was, rather than what would have happened in a specific counterfactual.
safe.x: Reading a working clock is safe. Reading one that stopped an hour ago is not, even when it happens to be right.
safe.q: A normally reliable visual system is used in a county where 99% of barn-looking objects are facades; you happen to look at the one real barn. Reliable process or safe belief?
safe.a: The visual process may be generally reliable, but this particular belief is unsafe because a tiny change in where you looked would have produced the same belief falsely. Safety is local to the epistemic environment.

defeat.w: Justification is not permanent. New information can remove it, and it can do so in two structurally different ways that people constantly conflate. Pollock's distinction is the most immediately usable idea on this entire map for anyone whose job involves argument, because the two kinds call for completely different responses.
defeat.i: A rebutting defeater gives you reason to believe the claim is false. It meets the claim head-on and the two contest the same ground. An undercutting defeater does something stranger and more powerful. It grants your evidence entirely and denies that the evidence supports the conclusion. It attacks the connection rather than either endpoint. After a successful undercutter, you are not left believing the opposite — you are left with no belief at all, which is often the more damaging outcome. The classic pair: you see a widget that looks red. Rebutting — someone produces a spectrometer reading showing it is blue.
defeat.x: Rebutting: someone shows the widget is actually blue. Undercutting: someone shows the room's lighting distorts colour, so your observation never established anything.
defeat.q: You present a result. A reviewer says the sample was drawn from a period of unusual volatility. Which defeater is that, and what would a good response look like?
defeat.a: Undercutting. They have not claimed your result is false or produced a contrary estimate; they have claimed your data cannot support the inference because the period is unrepresentative. Responding with more analysis of the same period misses it entirely. A good response either shows the result holds outside that period, shows the volatility does not bear on this particular inference, or concedes the scope restriction — which is a real concession, not a defeat.

kinds.w: Analytic epistemology concentrates on propositional knowledge—knowing that P—but much real expertise is practical or acquaintance-based. The distinction explains why excellent performers cannot always articulate rules, and why reading every procedure does not produce institutional competence. It also limits how far JTB-style analyses can be generalized.
kinds.i: Propositional knowledge (knowing that something is so), ability knowledge (knowing how to do something), and knowledge by acquaintance (knowing a person or a place). Epistemology studies mostly the first, which is a real limitation of the field.
kinds.x: Knowing that a bicycle stays upright by countersteering, versus knowing how to ride one. Neither gives you the other.
kinds.q: A senior analyst can diagnose a bad specification almost instantly but struggles to state a rule that junior staff can apply. Which kind of knowledge is most salient?
kinds.a: Knowing-how or tacit practical knowledge. The inability to fully propositionalize the skill does not show the expertise is unreal; it shows why institutional knowledge can be hard to transfer.

value.w: If true belief already gets you the right answer, what extra value does knowledge add? Plato’s Meno makes the puzzle vivid: a true opinion can guide you to Larissa just as well as knowledge on that trip. Any theory of knowledge should explain why the more demanding state is distinctively worth having.
value.i: Socrates asks Meno a question that has never been fully answered. If a true belief about the road to Larissa gets you to Larissa exactly as well as knowledge does, why is knowledge worth more? The standard answer is stability. A true belief that is merely true can drift away under pressure or fail to reproduce next time. Knowledge, because it is anchored to whatever made it non-accidental, tends to stay put and tends to repeat.
value.x: A correct guess and a well-founded judgment give the same answer today. Tomorrow, on a slightly different question, they do not.
value.q: Two analysts make the same correct forecast. One used a robust method; the other guessed. Today’s decision is identical. What is the Meno-style reason to prefer the first?
value.a: The first success is tied to a method or competence that can guide future cases; the second is detachable luck. The value problem asks a theory of knowledge to explain that extra value rather than merely assert it.

just.w: Truth alone cannot distinguish knowledge from a lucky guess. “Justification” names the missing normative dimension, but it immediately splits into two questions: what is justification supposed to mean, and what properties actually produce it? Evidentialists, reliabilists, virtue theorists, foundationalists, coherentists, internalists, and externalists answer the second question differently because they often emphasize different parts of the first.
just.i: Whatever it is that makes a true belief non-accidentally true — the most contested concept in the field, because everything else depends on how you settle it. Two questions have to be kept apart. First, what do we mean by justification? Second, what actually makes beliefs justified? Disagreements about the second are merely verbal if the parties have different answers to the first.
just.x: Two people believe the same true thing. One can show their work; the other guessed. Something separates them, and “justification” is the name for it.
just.q: Two analysts make the same correct forecast; one used a validated model and the other guessed. What does “justification” mark?
just.a: It marks the epistemic difference in the basis or process of belief. Both are true, but only the first has the sort of support that makes being right non-arbitrary—even though Gettier reminds us that justification alone may still not eliminate all luck.

evid.w: Evidentialism gives an intuitive internalist answer to “what makes belief rational?”: believe according to your evidence. It separates epistemic evaluation from whether the world cooperates—two agents with the same evidence have the same epistemic obligations even if only one happens to be right.
evid.i: A belief is justified to exactly the degree it fits the evidence you possess — where your evidence consists of your own mental states: perceptual, memorial, introspective and intuitional experiences.
evid.x: The coffee tastes sweet to you. That experience is your evidence that the coffee is sweet.
evid.q: Two analysts have exactly the same dataset and background information but live in different worlds where the data-generating process differs. According to evidentialism, can one be more justified solely because her hidden world is friendlier?
evid.a: No. If their evidence is genuinely the same, evidentialism gives them the same justificatory status. The difference in hidden reliability matters to an externalist, not to evidential fit as such.

reliab.w: Gettier and animal knowledge both pressure the idea that justification must consist in reasons available to reflection. Reliabilism externalizes the condition: vision, memory, or another process can justify because it reliably produces true beliefs, not because the subject can supply an argument that it does.
reliab.i: A belief is justified if it was produced by a process that tends to yield truths — whether or not you can articulate why, and whether or not you have any access to the fact that it is reliable.
reliab.x: Vision is reliable, so your visual beliefs are justified even if you have never thought about optics for a second.
reliab.q: A model class has a strong long-run record, but you have concrete evidence that today’s input pipeline is corrupted. Does bare process reliabilism automatically license the output?
reliab.a: A very simple version may, which exposes the problem. A defensible reliabilist account must accommodate defeaters or specify the relevant process narrowly enough that “model-plus-corrupted-pipeline” is not reliable.

intext.w: The dispute separates two intuitions that often travel together: a person should be able to give reasons for a belief, and a belief-forming method should actually connect them to truth. Internalism prioritizes the first-person perspective; externalism prioritizes the objective quality of the process. Gettier cases, clairvoyance cases, and ordinary reliance on perception make the tension unavoidable.
intext.i: Internalism holds that whatever justifies you is always recognisable on reflection. Externalism denies it: what justifies you can be a fact about the world — such as the reliability of your faculties — to which you have no access at all.
intext.x: A perfectly reliable clairvoyant who has no idea they are reliable. Justified, or not? Your answer places you on one side.
intext.q: An analyst uses a procedure that is in fact highly reliable but cannot explain why it works. What different questions do internalism and externalism ask?
intext.a: Internalism asks whether the analyst has accessible grounds that make the belief reasonable from the inside. Externalism asks whether the procedure actually has the right truth-conducive relation to the world.

deont.w: This conception connects epistemology to blame, permission, and intellectual responsibility. Its central difficulty is control: duties normally govern actions we can choose, while belief often arrives involuntarily. The view therefore forces a distinction between direct control over belief and indirect control over inquiry, attention, evidence-seeking, and habits.
deont.i: Justification understood as duty-fulfilment: you are justified in believing p if you are under no obligation to refrain from believing it. This immediately raises whether belief is voluntary at all.
deont.x: Try to decide, right now, to believe that it is snowing outside. You cannot do it by deciding.
deont.q: Someone reaches a false conclusion after checking all available evidence carefully and following a reasonable method. What does a deontological view tend to say?
deont.a: They may still be epistemically justified or blameless because they fulfilled their epistemic duties, even though the belief is false and the process may later turn out to need improvement.

basicality.w: Foundationalism often wins too easily if “basic” is left ambiguous. Doxastic basicality describes the belief’s psychological ancestry; epistemic basicality describes the structure of its justification. A perceptual belief may arise non-inferentially yet still be justified only if background conditions about perception, lighting, competence, or normality obtain.
basicality.i: Two different senses of “basic”. Doxastic: the belief is not justified by any other belief. Epistemic: the belief's justification does not depend on your having justification for any further proposition. The second is much stricter.
basicality.x: A perceptual belief may rest on no other belief, yet still depend on your having grounds to trust perception in the first place.
basicality.q: You immediately believe the gauge reads 40, but your justification depends on the gauge being calibrated. Doxastically basic? Epistemically basic?
basicality.a: Doxastically basic, because you did not infer the reading from another belief. Not obviously epistemically basic, because its justification depends on the calibration/reliability condition.

truth.w: Knowledge is factive, yet theories disagree about what truth itself amounts to—correspondence with reality, coherence, pragmatic success, or a thin logical role. These theories are not interchangeable because they handle realism, disagreement, unobservable claims, and framework dependence differently.
truth.i: Knowledge is justified true belief — so the whole edifice rests on a concept most people never examine. What makes a proposition true? Four families of answer compete. Truth as correspondence to how things are; truth as coherence within a system; truth as what works under sustained inquiry; and the deflationary view that truth is not a substantive property at all, so the question dissolves. Skipping this while studying justification is like doing cost-benefit analysis without defining the benefit.
truth.x: “Snow is white” is true. Because of snow? Because it fits everything else you believe? Because acting on it works? Each answer builds a different discipline.
truth.q: Why doesn’t a correspondence theory by itself tell you whether today’s inflation estimate is true?
truth.a: Because it says what would make the proposition true—the relevant worldly state—not how to know that state. Measurement, inference, and justification are separate epistemic problems.

corr.w: Knowledge requires truth, so a natural question is what makes a proposition true. Correspondence theory gives the realist answer: beliefs and sentences do not become true because they are coherent, useful, or accepted; they are true because the world has the relevant facts or states of affairs.
corr.i: A proposition is true when it corresponds to how things actually stand, independently of what anyone believes. Aristotle's formulation is still the clearest: to say of what is that it is, is true. This is the default assumption of empirical work, and it is what gives evidence its point. If truth were not answerable to the world, gathering data would be a strange thing to do.
corr.x: “The bridge is 400 metres long” is true if and only if the bridge is 400 metres long.
corr.q: A perfectly coherent economic model says unemployment is 4%, but the actual population state makes the relevant statistic 6%. What does correspondence theory say?
corr.a: The 4% proposition is false despite coherence. What makes the proposition true or false is the relevant worldly state, not its fit with the rest of the model.

cohtruth.w: Correspondence invites the question of how beliefs can be compared with a reality outside the belief system. Coherence theories answer by locating truth in systematic fit: consistency, mutual implication, and explanatory integration within the best overall system.
cohtruth.i: A proposition is true when it belongs to a maximally coherent system of propositions. Truth is a property of the fit, not of a relation to something outside.
cohtruth.x: Mathematical truth looks like this — consistency with the axioms, not correspondence to objects in a field somewhere.
cohtruth.q: Two macro models are internally coherent and both fit the observed sample, but imply opposite counterfactual policies. Why is that especially hard for a coherence theory of truth?
cohtruth.a: Because internal coherence does not select between incompatible coherent systems. The theory needs a principled story about total-system coherence or some reality constraint; otherwise both look equally truth-conferring.

prag.w: The pragmatic tradition rejects the idea that truth is useful only as a static relation between sentence and world. Beliefs are tools inside inquiry. Their meaning and epistemic significance emerge in the consequences of acting, testing, and revising over time.
prag.i: A belief is true if it works — if acting on it succeeds, and if it is the belief inquiry would converge on in the long run. Peirce's version ties truth to the end point of investigation, not to present usefulness.
prag.x: “This bridge design holds” is true if bridges built that way do not fall down.
prag.q: A false but morale-boosting forecast improves a team’s effort for one quarter. Does that make it true on a serious pragmatic theory?
prag.a: No. Short-run utility is not enough. The belief must survive disciplined inquiry and the broader consequences of experience; a claim that works only by masking reality is exactly what longer-run inquiry should expose.

defl.w: Traditional theories ask for the nature of truth—correspondence, coherence, or practical success. Deflationists suspect the question is overinflated. The truth predicate performs logical and linguistic jobs, especially generalization, without requiring a substantial metaphysical property called Truth.
defl.i: “It is true that p” says nothing beyond p itself. Truth is a logical convenience — it lets us generalise and endorse — not a substantive property in need of analysis.
defl.x: “It's true that it's raining” adds nothing at all to “it's raining”.
defl.q: Why is “everything in this report is true” useful if “p is true” adds nothing to p in each individual case?
defl.a: Because the truth predicate lets you endorse many propositions at once without listing or even being able to formulate each one. Deflationism calls that logical-expressive role real while denying a deep metaphysical property is needed.

object.w: Disagreement often slides from “people use different standards” to “there is no fact of the matter.” This concept exists to separate sociological plurality, epistemic dependence on methods, and metaphysical relativity. The question is not whether perspectives influence inquiry—they do—but whether truth itself varies with perspective.
object.i: Whether claims are true full stop, or true only relative to a framework, paradigm, or culture. The question sharpens once you take theory-ladenness and incommensurability seriously.
object.x: Are scientific claims true, or true within the system of thought that produced them?
object.q: Two agencies use different thresholds for “material risk” but agree on all underlying probabilities and consequences. Is the disagreement automatically about relative truth?
object.a: No. It may be a normative or classificatory disagreement about standards. Relativism about truth would be a much stronger claim—that incompatible propositions are true relative to different frameworks.

sources.w: Every belief must enter or persist in a cognitive system somehow. If we demand an independent proof of each source before trusting it, the proof must itself come from a source and regress begins. The practical theory therefore needs prima facie entitlement plus characteristic defeaters for each channel.
sources.i: Beliefs arise from many causes, most of them disreputable — desire, fear, habit, prejudice. Only a few sources are candidates for producing knowledge: perception, introspection, memory, reason, and testimony. Each raises the same shape of question. Why is this a source of justification at all? Is it because it is in fact reliable, or because we have grounds to believe it is, or because it could not be otherwise? Any evidentiary framework you have ever worked under is implicitly a ranking of these five.
sources.x: You know the room is cold by feeling it, that you ate breakfast by remembering, that 7+5=12 by reasoning, and the population of Brazil because someone told you.
sources.q: You remember a result, see a chart reproducing it, and read three articles repeating it—but all four ultimately derive from the same flawed original measurement. How many independent source types protect you?
sources.a: Potentially none in the relevant evidential sense. Memory, perception of the chart, and testimony are distinct channels, but if their information all traces to the same flawed observation, the epistemic dependence remains one-source deep.

percep.w: Most empirical knowledge begins with perception, so epistemology cannot require us to prove the senses reliable before using them without generating a regress. Yet illusion, hallucination, and variation in viewpoint show that appearance is not infallible. The problem is to explain defeasible perceptual entitlement.
percep.i: Knowledge through the senses, and the oldest puzzle in the theory of knowledge. When you see a tomato, do you see the tomato, or do you see something else — an appearance, an image, a sense-datum — from which the tomato is inferred? The question is not idle. If perception delivers the world directly, observation can be foundational. If it delivers only representations, then every observation is already an inference, and the gap between data and world is permanent.
percep.x: A straight stick looks bent in water. The experience is of something bent — so what did you directly perceive?
percep.q: A measurement display looks red, but you learn the room is illuminated by red light. What happened to the perceptual justification?
percep.a: It is undercut. The experience still occurred, but the new information breaks the link between red-looking and being red. Perception supplies prima facie, defeasible justification, not an indefeasible guarantee.

dirreal.w: The theory preserves the common-sense idea that when you see a tree, the tree—not a mental image—is what you perceive. It matters because if perception is mediated by an object of awareness, a new skeptical gap opens: how do you know the intermediary accurately represents the world? Direct realism tries to block that gap at the starting point.
dirreal.i: We perceive external objects themselves, with no intermediary. Experience is a form of contact with the world, not a picture of it.
dirreal.x: When you see the tomato, what you see is the tomato. Nothing stands between.
dirreal.q: If a direct realist accepts that perception is neurally processed, what do they still deny?
dirreal.a: They deny that the immediate object of ordinary veridical perception must therefore be an inner representation or sense-datum from which the external object is only inferred.

indreal.w: The view explains illusion, perspective, and sensory processing by distinguishing the object from the way it is represented. Its price is epistemic distance. Once access is through a representation, the theory must explain how the representation is known to correspond to a mind-independent cause rather than becoming a self-contained screen.
indreal.i: We perceive external objects only by perceiving something else that represents them. What you directly access is the representation; the object is an inference from it.
indreal.x: What reaches you is the image. The object behind it is a hypothesis you did not consciously form.
indreal.q: Why does indirect realism solve one problem of perception only by creating another?
indreal.a: It handles illusion by placing a representation between subject and object, but that creates the further problem of explaining how the subject can know the representation accurately corresponds to the external world.

illus.w: Illusion creates pressure on direct realism. If a straight stick looks bent in water, and a genuinely bent stick can look the same, what is common to the two experiences? Traditional indirect theories answer: an appearance, sense-datum, or representation. The argument matters because the proposed common factor can insert a skeptical veil between mind and world.
illus.i: Illusions and veridical perceptions can be subjectively indistinguishable. So whatever we directly perceive must be the same kind of thing in both cases — and since it cannot be the object in the illusion case, it is never the object.
illus.q: A measurement instrument produces the same display both when the target is present and when an artifact is present. What is the epistemic analogue of the argument from illusion?
illus.a: The output alone does not reveal which underlying state generated it. You need an account of the measurement relation or independent checks; identical appearance does not guarantee identical reality.

mem.w: Without memory, almost no extended reasoning or knowledge would survive from one moment to the next. The epistemic problem is whether memory creates new justification or merely carries forward earlier justification, and how to distinguish genuine remembering from a present memory-like experience.
mem.i: The capacity to retain knowledge already acquired. Remembering that p entails that p is true; merely seeming to remember does not, and from the inside the two can feel identical.
mem.x: You seem to recall locking the door. Did you actually, or are you remembering the habit?
mem.q: You remember a coefficient estimate but no longer remember the dataset, specification, or whether the result survived robustness checks. What epistemic status does the memory have?
mem.a: It may preserve the fact that you once believed the estimate, but high confidence in the current number does not recreate the missing grounds. For consequential use, the loss of provenance is a reason to re-check rather than treat memory vividness as evidence.

past.w: Memory, documents, fossils, and databases are all present states used to infer earlier states. Russell’s five-minute hypothesis dramatizes the logical gap: the current world could in principle have appeared with all apparent traces already in place. The point is not that this happened, but that ordinary historical knowledge relies on anti-skeptical assumptions about memory, causation, and temporal continuity.
past.i: Nothing in present experience entails that the past actually occurred. Russell's five-minute hypothesis: the universe could have sprung into existence five minutes ago, complete with fossils, records, and memories.
past.q: What does the five-minute hypothesis actually establish, if anything?
past.a: Not that the world is five minutes old. It establishes that present traces do not deductively entail the ordinary past; trusting the past depends on explanatory, causal, and memory assumptions.

intro.w: Foundationalists are drawn to introspection because “I am in pain” or “it seems red to me” appears to need no inference from the external world. If any source can provide non-inferential justification, first-person awareness is a leading candidate. The difficulty is specifying how strong that privilege really is.
intro.i: Knowledge of your own mental states. Long treated as specially privileged — infallible, indubitable, or incorrigible — and therefore the favourite candidate for a foundation.
intro.x: Can you be wrong that you have a headache? It feels impossible — until you try to distinguish an unpleasant itch from a mild pain.
intro.q: You say “I am anxious because of the meeting.” Which part has the stronger introspective claim: being anxious, or the causal explanation?
intro.a: The occurrent anxiety has the stronger first-person claim. The explanation of why you are anxious is an interpretation and may depend on inference, background beliefs, or confabulation.

apriori.w: Some truths seem knowable without checking the world: logical entailments, elementary mathematics, and conceptual constraints. The a priori matters because it determines whether experience is the source of all substantive knowledge and what status to assign to mathematics, logic, and theoretical reasoning.
apriori.i: Justification that does not depend on experience at all. Mathematics, logic, and conceptual truths are the paradigm cases: you do not survey bachelors to learn that they are unmarried. Three questions follow. Does a priori knowledge exist, or is all knowledge ultimately empirical? If it exists, what produces it — intellectual insight, grasp of necessity, or a reliable cognitive process? And how far does it extend?
apriori.x: “If a ball is green all over, it does not have black spots.” No observation is required, and none would help.
apriori.q: You know that no object can be both entirely green and entirely black at the same place and time without inspecting every object. What feature makes the justification a priori?
apriori.a: The warrant comes from conceptual or rational relations, not an inductive survey of colored objects. Experience may be needed to acquire the concepts, but not to justify this particular relation.

ratemp.w: The dispute asks where intellectual content comes from and therefore what theory can legitimately do before data arrive. It is the background fault line beneath arguments about innate concepts, mathematics, causation, economic models, and whether conceptual necessity can tell us anything about the world.
ratemp.i: The organising dispute of early modern philosophy. Rationalists hold that reason alone can deliver substantive knowledge of the world. Empiricists hold that all such knowledge ultimately traces back to experience, and that reason only rearranges what experience supplies. The argument was never settled; it was absorbed. Every methodological fight about whether to start from theory or from data is a descendant of it.
ratemp.x: Is “every event has a cause” known by thinking it through, or generalised from a very large number of observations?
ratemp.q: An economist says a theorem reveals a substantive feature of any possible market even before observing one. Which side bears the burden, and what must be shown?
ratemp.a: That is a rationalist-style claim. The burden is to show that the theorem’s premises are not merely chosen definitions or empirical assumptions in disguise, and that the result legitimately applies to the world.

ansyn.w: The distinction matters because it separates what a framework builds in by definition from what experience teaches us. Without it, deductions from chosen definitions can be mistaken for discoveries. Quine’s attack matters equally: if meaning itself is embedded in a revisable web, the neat division between “definition” and “fact” may be less absolute than classical empiricism assumed.
ansyn.i: Analytic truths are true in virtue of meaning alone; synthetic truths say something substantive about the world. “All bachelors are unmarried” versus “most bachelors own cars”. Quine's 1951 attack argued the distinction cannot be drawn without circularity, and that no statement is immune from revision in the light of experience — including the ones we call definitional.
ansyn.x: Is “force equals mass times acceleration” a definition of force or an empirical discovery? The answer has changed over time, which is Quine's point.
ansyn.q: Your index rises because its definition mechanically gives larger weight to a component that rose. Is the increase an empirical discovery about the system or partly analytic?
ansyn.a: Partly analytic: some of the result follows from how the index was defined. The empirical content lies in the component movements and in whether the chosen definition validly represents the target concept.

synapr.w: Kant needed a category that could explain how mathematics and fundamental principles of experience seem both informative and necessary. If all a priori truths are merely analytic, reason cannot add substantive knowledge; if all synthetic truths require experience, necessity becomes difficult to explain. The synthetic a priori is the attempted bridge.
synapr.i: Kant's claim that some propositions are both informative about the world and knowable without experience. If the category is real, some substantive knowledge is available before any data arrives.
synapr.q: A model proves a result from axioms without data. What additional claim would be needed to call the result synthetic a priori rather than merely analytic-relative-to-the-axioms?
synapr.a: You would need to show that the result provides substantive knowledge of the world and is justified independently of experience—not merely that it follows necessarily from stipulated premises.

testim.w: Most of what anyone knows—history, science, geography, institutions, even today’s news—comes from others. If testimony were epistemically parasitic on personal verification, ordinary knowledge would collapse. The theory therefore asks when another person’s word gives prima facie reason and when independent checking is required.
testim.i: Coming to know something because somebody said so. It is by far the largest source of what you believe, and the one that gets the least scrutiny. The puzzle: why is testimony a source of knowledge at all? If it is because the speaker is reliable, then a reliable speaker whose reliability is completely unknown to you should still transmit knowledge — which seems wrong. If it requires evidence of reliability, almost nothing you believe qualifies, because you cannot audit the sources of most of what you know.
testim.x: You know the population of Brazil, the boiling point of mercury, and what happened in 1789. You verified none of them.
testim.q: Three respected reports agree, but all ultimately cite the same unnamed official. How many independent testimonial supports do you have?
testim.a: Probably one evidential lineage, not three. Agreement raises confidence only to the extent that the sources’ information is genuinely independent or independently validated.

reduct.w: We cannot personally verify most of what we know, so testimony needs a default policy. Humean reductionism asks us to ground trust in observed reliability, analogy, and independent evidence. Reidian anti-reductionism argues that such evidence is impossible to obtain without already trusting testimony, so acceptance must begin as a defeasible entitlement.
reduct.i: Reductionism: trust in testimony must be earned by independent evidence of the speaker's reliability. Anti-reductionism: trust is a default entitlement, withdrawn only when a specific defeater appears.
reduct.x: Do you need grounds to believe a stranger's directions, or only grounds to doubt them?
reduct.q: You accept a new data vendor only after independently validating its historical accuracy. Which side does that procedure resemble?
reduct.a: A reductionist posture: testimonial/data-source trust is earned by independent evidence of reliability rather than granted as the default.

reid.w: A child learns language and almost everything else by accepting others long before they can independently certify speaker reliability. Reid turns that developmental fact into an epistemic insight: if trust required prior evidence in every case, the evidence needed to establish reliability could never get started. Social knowledge therefore begins with defeasible credulity, not universal suspicion.
reid.i: Reid argued that by our very constitution we accept testimony and attribute credibility, unless we encounter a specific reason not to. Trust is the starting state, not an achievement.
reid.x: Children believe what they are told before they can assess anyone's reliability — and mostly end up right.
reid.q: Why is “verify every source before believing anything it says” difficult as a universal rule?
reid.a: Because the verification itself depends on prior testimony, language, records, and trusted methods. A Reidian view says some defeasible trust must be epistemically prior to the verification system.

skep.w: Skeptical arguments expose hidden standards. The brain-in-a-vat case, closure, relevant alternatives, contextualism, Moorean reversal, and Cartesian versus Pyrrhonian strategies are different moves in one architecture: which possibilities must be excluded, and what happens when they cannot be?
skep.i: How far knowledge actually reaches, and the arguments that it reaches far less than we assume. Nobody seriously believes the sceptical conclusion. The interest lies in the fact that the arguments for it are made of premises everyone accepts. That is what makes this branch the most transferable material on the map. The closure principle, the relevant-alternatives move, and the Moorean reversal are tools you can use in an ordinary argument tomorrow.
skep.x: You think you know you have hands. A sceptic will grant you everything except the ability to rule out a scenario in which you do not.
skep.q: A critic raises a one-in-a-billion alternative and says you no longer “know.” What is the first architectural question?
skep.a: Which theory of relevance or knowledge standards makes that alternative epistemically live? The debate is not settled by its mere logical possibility; closure, relevant alternatives, and contextualism answer that question differently.

biv.w: Ordinary knowledge seems to require that our evidence discriminate truth from relevant error. A brain in a vat receives exactly the same experiences as a normal embodied person, so sensory evidence cannot distinguish the two. The scenario concentrates Cartesian skepticism into a modern external-world test.
biv.i: The argument in three lines. (1) You do not know that you are not a brain in a vat. (2) If you do not know that, you do not know that you have hands. Therefore (3) you do not know that you have hands. Premise (1) holds because your evidence would be identical either way — that is built into the hypothesis. Premise (2) follows from the closure principle. The argument is valid, its premises are plausible, and its conclusion is unacceptable. Something has to give, and the whole literature is about what.
biv.x: Envatted, everything looks and feels exactly as it does now. That is the point: evidence cannot distinguish the two cases.
biv.q: Why can’t ordinary sensory evidence—“I see my hands”—by itself settle whether you are a normal person or a perfectly deceived BIV?
biv.a: Because the scenario is constructed so the sensory evidence is the same in both cases. The dispute therefore moves to whether knowledge requires ruling out that alternative, not to gathering more of the same kind of sensory evidence.

closure.w: Closure captures the intuition that knowledge is preserved by known entailment. It also powers the skeptical argument: if having hands entails not being a handless brain in a vat, then knowing you have hands appears to require knowing you are not such a brain.
closure.i: If you know p, and you know that p entails q, then you know q. Stated plainly it sounds almost too obvious to name. It is also the engine of the sceptical argument. You know you have hands; having hands entails not being a handless brain in a vat; so you know you are not one. Since the sceptic denies the conclusion, either closure or the first premise must go — and both are painful to give up.
closure.x: You know you had exactly two drinks. That entails fewer than three. So you know you had fewer than three. Closure at work, and clearly correct.
closure.q: You know a report contains exactly two material errors, and you know “exactly two” entails “fewer than three.” What does closure license?
closure.a: If you competently make the inference, it licenses knowledge that the report contains fewer than three material errors. The principle preserves knowledge through the known entailment.

relalt.w: Radical skepticism becomes overwhelming only if knowledge requires eliminating every possibility of error. Relevant-alternatives theory weakens that demand: to know an animal is a zebra you must rule out nearby ordinary alternatives, but perhaps not a fantastical zoo conspiracy unless the context makes it live.
relalt.i: Deny closure. To know something you need only rule out the relevant alternatives, and exotic sceptical scenarios are not relevant to ordinary claims.
relalt.x: To know it is a barn you must rule out a shed. You do not have to rule out a film-set facade unless you are in a county full of them.
relalt.q: You identify a barn in an ordinary county. Must you rule out Hollywood facades? What changes if you learn the county is used as a movie set?
relalt.a: In the ordinary county the facade possibility may be irrelevant. Once you learn the environment contains many facades, that alternative becomes live and must be discriminated; the same visual evidence may no longer suffice for knowledge.

moore.w: Sceptical arguments are valid and built from plausible premises, yet nobody believes their conclusions. That combination looks like a paradox demanding a technical solution. Moore's response reframes it: an argument is a transaction in credibility, and you are always entitled to run the transaction in whichever direction preserves more of it.
moore.i: Consider the sceptical argument: (1) I do not know I am not a brain in a vat; (2) if I do not know that, I do not know I have hands; so (3) I do not know I have hands. Moore observed that this can be turned around. Since I do know I have hands — and I know it far more securely than I know premise (1) — I may run modus tollens the other way and conclude that premise (1) is false. The general principle is what matters, and it generalises far past scepticism. Validity transmits credibility from premises to conclusion, but it also transmits incredibility backwards from conclusion to premises.
moore.x: Moore held up a hand and said: here is one. The gesture was the argument.
moore.q: A chain of individually reasonable modelling assumptions yields the result that a policy has no cost at all. You cannot find the error. What are you entitled to conclude?
moore.a: That at least one assumption is wrong, and you may say so publicly before locating it. The zero-cost conclusion is far less credible than any of the individual assumptions is credible, so the argument has refuted one of its own inputs rather than established its output. What you are not entitled to do is nominate a convenient assumption as the culprit without evidence — Moore licenses rejecting the conclusion, not choosing which premise to blame.

context.w: Ordinary life and skeptical philosophy seem to deliver opposite but plausible verdicts. In everyday contexts “I know the bank is open Saturday” is fine; once a costly error or skeptical possibility is salient, the same evidence feels insufficient. Contextualism explains both without saying the subject’s evidence changed.
context.i: What the word “know” means shifts with the conversational context, and specifically with which error possibilities have been made salient. In a low-standards context ordinary evidence suffices. Once someone raises a serious-sounding possibility of error, the standard rises and the same evidence no longer suffices. This preserves closure — the principle holds at every standard — while explaining why both the sceptic and the ordinary speaker seem right in their own settings.
context.x: In the pub you know the bank opens on Saturday. In a conversation about missing a mortgage payment, suddenly you do not — and nothing about your evidence changed.
context.q: At lunch you say, “I know the bank is open tomorrow.” Later you realize missing the visit would trigger a foreclosure deadline and now hesitate. What does contextualism say changed?
context.a: The operative standard for correctly attributing knowledge rose because the cost and error possibilities became salient. The underlying evidence can remain exactly the same.

pyrrh.w: This is a different skeptical ambition from Cartesian doubt. The Pyrrhonist avoids the self-defeating claim “nothing can be known,” because that too would be a doctrine. Instead, arguments and counterarguments are balanced until assent is withheld. Suspension—epoché—is treated as an achievement of disciplined non-commitment.
pyrrh.i: Ancient scepticism did not aim to prove that we know nothing. It aimed at epoché — suspension of judgment — and the tranquillity said to follow from ceasing to insist.
pyrrh.x: For any argument, an equally strong opposing argument can be found. So neither is asserted, and assent is withheld.
pyrrh.q: After examining two technically serious but balanced arguments, you deliberately decline to assert either conclusion. What would a Pyrrhonist say you achieved?
pyrrh.a: Epoché—suspension of judgment. The achievement lies in resisting a claim that outruns the available asymmetry in reasons, not in proving both sides false.

cartes.w: The Cartesian project asks whether certainty can be rebuilt after granting the strongest skeptical possibilities. Doubt the senses, dreaming, even mathematics under an evil deceiver; if a belief survives that procedure, it has a special claim to foundational status.
cartes.i: Methodical doubt: discard everything that can possibly be doubted in order to find something that cannot, and rebuild from there. The evil demon is the instrument that makes the doubt total.
cartes.x: Doubt the senses, doubt mathematics, doubt the external world — and arrive at the one thing doubting itself cannot touch.
cartes.q: Why is “I am now thinking” harder for the Cartesian skeptic to doubt than “there is a table in front of me”?
cartes.a: A deceiver could cause the table experience without a table, but the very occurrence of being deceived or doubting is itself a thinking event. The attempt to doubt it instantiates what is being asserted.

formal.w: Binary belief throws away information when evidence is partial. Probability provides a language for degrees of confidence, while Bayes, likelihood ratios, Dutch-book arguments, calibration, and scoring rules turn vague advice like “update appropriately” into explicit constraints and measurable performance.
formal.i: Using the tools of probability and logic to model belief and evidence. The founding move is to stop treating belief as a switch and start treating it as a dial: a credence between 0 and 1. That single change makes a great deal tractable. Evidence stops being something that proves or fails to prove and becomes something that moves you, by an amount you can specify. Disagreement stops being a clash of positions and becomes a difference in priors or in information.
formal.x: Not “do I believe it?” but “how confident am I, and what evidence would move that number, and by how much?”
formal.q: A model reports “73.4%” but the hypothesis space omits a plausible structural break. What formal-epistemic question comes before admiring the precision?
formal.a: Whether the probability model represents the relevant uncertainty at all. Internal coherence inside a misspecified hypothesis space does not remove model uncertainty; sensitivity and alternative models are part of the epistemic audit.

cred.w: Most real uncertainty is not binary. You may regard rain tomorrow as 40% likely without either believing or disbelieving it outright. Formal epistemology uses credences to model partial belief, connect evidence to decision, and make calibration and updating mathematically assessable.
cred.i: Treating belief as a degree between 0 and 1 rather than an on/off state. Ramsey's move: your credence is revealed by the bets you would accept.
cred.x: You neither believe nor disbelieve that it will rain tomorrow. You are at about 0.4, and you act accordingly.
cred.q: You say “I don’t believe the policy will pass, but I’d put it at 45%.” Is that incoherent?
cred.a: No. Binary belief and credence are different representations. You can withhold outright belief while assigning a substantial probability that guides decisions.

bayes.w: If belief is binary, evidence has to either establish a claim or fail to, and most real evidence does neither. Treating belief as a degree between 0 and 1 dissolves that. Evidence stops being a verdict and becomes a force with a magnitude — and the magnitude is calculable. This is the single most practically useful formal result in epistemology.
bayes.i: Learn the odds form, because it is the only version you can run in your head during a conversation: prior odds × likelihood ratio = posterior odds. The likelihood ratio asks how much more probable this observation is if the hypothesis is true than if it is false. Two disciplines fall out immediately. First, you must have had a prior. If you cannot state roughly what you believed before seeing the evidence, you were not updating, you were reacting — and you have no way to say how much the evidence moved you. Second, evidence that is equally expected under both hypotheses has a ratio near one and therefore moves nothing, however impressive it looks.
bayes.x: A rare disease, an accurate test, a positive result — and the posterior probability is still low, because the prior was very low. The test did not fail; the intuition did.
bayes.q: A colleague says a new finding 'confirms' the model. What single question tells you how much it actually confirms it?
bayes.a: How likely was this finding if the model were wrong? That is the denominator of the likelihood ratio, and it is the number nobody computes. If a rival account predicts the same finding roughly as strongly, the ratio is near one and the finding is decoration. Confirmation is not about fit with your hypothesis; it is about the gap between fit with yours and fit with the alternatives.

priors.w: Bayes’ theorem tells you exactly how to update from a prior, but it does not by itself tell you which prior to start with. Two coherent analysts can process the same likelihood and reach different posteriors because their initial odds differ. The formal rule therefore relocates rather than eliminates a foundational problem.
priors.i: Bayes tells you how to update but says nothing about where to start. So where does a prior come from? From another prior — regress. From the data it is supposed to weigh — circularity. Or from stipulation — an arbitrary stop. Those are the three horns again. Bayesianism does not escape the trilemma; it relocates it into a place where the choice is visible and auditable, which is a genuine gain and should be stated as such rather than as a solution.
priors.x: Two analysts, the same data, different priors, different conclusions — and both perfectly coherent. Nothing in the mathematics adjudicates between them.
priors.q: Two analysts use the same data and likelihood but report 20% and 70% posterior probabilities. What is the first diagnostic question?
priors.a: Ask for their priors—and then for prior sensitivity. Bayes does not make disagreement mysterious: posterior differences can be decomposed into starting odds and evidential likelihood ratios.

lr.w: Evidence does not support a hypothesis merely because the evidence is compatible with it. The decisive comparison is contrastive: would the same observation also be expected if the hypothesis were false or a rival were true? The likelihood ratio isolates that comparison.
lr.i: The strength of a piece of evidence is a ratio: how much more probable is this observation under one hypothesis than under its rival? Evidence that is equally expected either way has a ratio near 1 — it is not evidence at all.
lr.x: “The result is consistent with our theory.” Consistent with the rival theory too? Then the likelihood ratio is 1 and you have learned nothing.
lr.q: A finding had 60% probability under your model and 55% under the main rival. Is “our model predicted the finding” strong evidence?
lr.a: No. The likelihood ratio is about 1.09, barely above neutral. The finding fits your model, but it also fits the rival almost as well, so it discriminates very little.

dutch.w: Probability axioms can look like elegant mathematics with no reason that actual beliefs should obey them. Dutch-book arguments supply a normative bridge. If your stated degrees of belief violate coherence, another agent can exploit the inconsistency without needing to know which event occurs. Rationality therefore requires at least avoiding sure-loss combinations.
dutch.i: If your degrees of belief violate the probability axioms, a clever bookmaker can construct a set of bets you will each accept as fair and which together guarantee you a loss.
dutch.x: Hold that P(A) = 0.6 and P(not-A) = 0.6 and someone can take money from you with certainty, no luck required.
dutch.q: Two forecasters both obey all probability axioms, but one is consistently overconfident. Has the Dutch-book argument identified the problem?
dutch.a: No. Both may be internally coherent. The overconfidence is a calibration problem, which requires comparing forecasts with outcomes rather than merely checking algebraic consistency.

calib.w: Confidence is otherwise hard to audit. Calibration converts subjective probability into a track record: among forecasts called 70%, roughly seven in ten should resolve true. This makes overconfidence and underconfidence measurable and trainable rather than personality labels.
calib.i: A calibrated forecaster is one whose 70% predictions come true about 70% of the time. Calibration is measurable — the Brier score and the logarithmic score both do it — and it is trainable, which is the finding that makes this whole subject practical rather than decorative. Note that calibration is not the same as accuracy. You can be perfectly calibrated by saying 50% to everything. What you want is calibration plus resolution: confident predictions that turn out right.
calib.x: A forecaster who says 90% and is right 60% of the time is overconfident by a measurable, correctable amount.
calib.q: Across 100 forecasts labeled 80%, only 55 resolve true. What is the primary diagnosis?
calib.a: Systematic overconfidence at that probability level: the stated 80% events occurred about 55% of the time. You would still inspect sample composition and resolution, but the calibration gap is directly measurable.

probint.w: A number such as “30% chance” looks unambiguous until we ask what in the world the 30% refers to. Repeated frequencies fit repeatable events; propensity theories treat chance as a property of setups; logical interpretations treat probability as evidential relation; subjective Bayesians treat it as coherent credence. The interpretation determines what counts as evidence and what statements are meaningful.
probint.i: What a probability actually is: a long-run relative frequency, a physical propensity of a setup, a logical relation between propositions, or a rational agent's degree of belief.
probint.x: “A 30% chance of rain tomorrow” — but tomorrow happens exactly once. Which interpretation makes that sentence meaningful?
probint.q: What does “there is a 30% chance this firm defaults next year” mean if the event occurs only once?
probint.a: The sentence needs an interpretation: perhaps a calibrated credence, a model-based frequency over a reference class, or a propensity-like risk. The number alone does not settle the ontology.

lottery.w: A million-ticket lottery makes it rational to assign each ticket an overwhelming probability of losing, yet irrational to believe that every ticket will lose because you know one must win. The paradox exposes a mismatch between threshold accounts of belief and the logic of conjunction. Small individual risks accumulate across many claims.
lottery.i: A lottery with a million tickets. For each ticket you are rationally confident it will lose — 0.999999. Yet you know one of them wins, so you cannot believe of every ticket that it loses. The lesson is that high credence in each of many claims does not aggregate into belief in their conjunction. Confidence erodes multiplicatively, and fast.
lottery.x: Twenty claims, each 95% likely, independently. The probability that all twenty hold is about 36%.
lottery.q: Twenty independent claims are each 95% likely. Is it reasonable to treat the whole 20-claim package as 95% likely to be entirely correct?
lottery.a: No. Under independence the probability all twenty are correct is about 36%. High confidence in each item does not preserve high confidence in the conjunction.

preface.w: Authors reasonably believe each sentence they assert, yet experience tells them that long works almost certainly contain an error. The two attitudes are individually rational but jointly inconsistent under simple closure rules. The paradox exposes the tension between local justification and global fallibility.
preface.i: An author believes each individual claim in her book, and also believes — from long experience — that the book contains at least one error. Both attitudes are rational, and together they are inconsistent.
preface.x: The standard preface: “any remaining errors are my own.” It is a formal contradiction and nobody objects.
preface.q: Can “I stand behind every estimate in this report” and “I expect at least one estimate is wrong” both be rational?
preface.a: Yes, and that is the paradox. Each estimate may be individually well supported while accumulated fallibility makes the global error claim highly credible.

phsci.w: Science works astonishingly well, but no single slogan explains why. Popper captures risky testing, Duhem–Quine the bundle problem, Kuhn the historical structure of normal science, Lakatos the difference between productive and degenerating adjustment, and underdetermination the residual ambiguity of evidence.
phsci.i: Applied epistemology of empirical claims. What makes evidence good, what theory choice actually rests on, how sciences change, and whether their theories describe reality or merely organise it. For anyone doing quantitative work this is not a humanities elective. It is the formal description of your own method, and it names the failure modes you have already met without having words for them.
phsci.x: Why does a controlled trial license a conclusion that an anecdote does not, when both are observations?
phsci.q: A theory misses a prediction, its defenders alter an auxiliary, and the altered model later correctly predicts a novel result. Which sequence of concepts best diagnoses the episode?
phsci.a: Duhem–Quine explains why an auxiliary can be changed; Popper supplies the pressure to expose the theory to risk; Lakatos judges the repair progressive because it produced novel empirical success.

demarc.w: The question matters institutionally because “scientific” affects credibility, funding, regulation, and public authority. Falsifiability was the most famous answer, but historical and methodological work showed that sciences use heterogeneous methods and often protect theories through anomalies. The modern lesson is to assess a bundle of epistemic practices rather than worship one test.
demarc.i: What separates science from non-science? Falsifiability was the most famous proposed criterion; the consensus now is that no single criterion does the job cleanly.
demarc.x: Astrology makes predictions and revises them. So why is it not science?
demarc.q: A forecasting system makes precise falsifiable predictions but repeatedly patches its model after misses and publishes no independent validation. Has falsifiability settled its scientific status?
demarc.a: No. It passes one condition while failing others that matter: progressive prediction, transparency, independence, and response to error. Demarcation requires a broader methodological assessment.

induct.w: Induction is how empirical science moves from observed cases to general laws, future cases, and unseen populations. Hume’s problem is that the move cannot be justified deductively, and justifying it by saying induction has worked in the past is itself an inductive argument. The method that generates most empirical knowledge therefore lacks the kind of proof deduction enjoys.
induct.i: Hume's argument is short and has never been answered. Inductive inference assumes the future will resemble the past. That assumption cannot be established deductively, since its denial is not contradictory. Nor can it be established inductively, since that would use the very principle in question. So every empirical generalisation you have ever made rests on something you cannot justify. This is not a reason to stop generalising; it is a reason to know what you are doing when you do.
induct.x: The sun has risen every morning in recorded history. That fact entails nothing whatsoever about tomorrow morning.
induct.q: You have observed a stable coefficient for 20 years. What, strictly speaking, does those 20 years deductively entail about year 21?
induct.a: Nothing about the coefficient’s year-21 value follows deductively. Using the past pattern to project forward is an inductive move whose rationality depends on assumptions about stability, similarity, and the data-generating process.

grue.w: Hume asks why any past regularity should continue. Goodman sharpens the puzzle: even granting projection, the same observations support multiple incompatible generalizations depending on how we describe the pattern. The missing ingredient is not more data but a theory of which predicates are lawlike or natural.
grue.i: Goodman defines a predicate: something is grue if it is observed before time t and green, or observed after t and blue. Every emerald examined so far is both green and grue. So the same evidence supports “all emeralds are green” and “all emeralds are grue” equally — yet these predict opposite things about tomorrow. The riddle is not about colour. It shows that evidence alone never selects a generalisation. Some prior judgment about which predicates are projectible — which categories are natural — is doing the work, and that judgment is not in the data.
grue.x: Two specifications fit the same series identically and diverge sharply out of sample. The data cannot tell you which variables were the natural ones.
grue.q: Two transformations of the same dataset fit every historical observation exactly but imply opposite out-of-sample trends. What Goodman-style question should you ask?
grue.a: What makes one representation genuinely projectible rather than merely an equally fitting redescription? The answer must come from structure, mechanism, background theory, or a principled simplicity/naturalness constraint—not historical fit alone.

raven.w: “All ravens are black” is logically equivalent to “all non-black things are non-ravens.” If evidence confirms logically equivalent statements equally, observing a green apple appears to confirm that all ravens are black. The paradox forces confirmation theory to distinguish mere consistency and logical equivalence from evidential weight.
raven.i: “All ravens are black” is logically equivalent to “all non-black things are non-ravens”. Anything confirming the second confirms the first. So a green apple confirms that all ravens are black.
raven.x: Ornithology conducted indoors, by examining fruit. The logic is impeccable and the conclusion is absurd.
raven.q: Does finding a white shoe confirm “all ravens are black”?
raven.a: On many Bayesian accounts, technically yes but by an almost vanishing amount. The important lesson is that logical confirmation need not imply practically meaningful evidential weight.

popper.w: Hume had shown that no number of observations can establish a universal claim. The logical positivists tried to live with this by making verification the criterion of meaning, which quietly excluded most of physics. Popper's move was to stop trying to solve the problem of induction and instead route around it: if confirmation is impossible but refutation is not, build the whole method on refutation.
