popper.i: The asymmetry is the engine. 'All swans are white' cannot be established by any finite number of white swans, because the next one might differ. But a single black swan settles it, conclusively, by simple logic — this is modus tollens applied to a universal statement. From that asymmetry everything else follows. A good theory is not one that fits the evidence, since a vague theory fits everything. A good theory forbids a great deal: it makes risky predictions that could easily have failed. Science advances not by accumulating support but by eliminating error, and a theory that has survived severe testing is not thereby probable — it is merely still standing.
popper.x: No number of white swans establishes “all swans are white”. One black swan settles it, permanently.
popper.q: A model has been adjusted four times in ten years, each time after a missed forecast, and it now fits the whole history. Is it falsifiable?
popper.a: Almost certainly yes, in the trivial sense — you can still state observations that would contradict it. That is why the question is the wrong one. The right question is Lakatos's: did each adjustment predict something new that then turned out true, or did it only absorb what had already gone wrong? Four post-hoc patches with no novel predictions is a degenerating programme, whatever its formal falsifiability.

risky.w: Evidence is more informative when the observed outcome would have been surprising under the theory’s rivals or when the theory exposed itself to genuine failure. Popper emphasizes risk because flexible theories can accumulate apparent confirmations cheaply. Specificity, pre-specification, and low probability of success by chance make a passed test epistemically valuable.
risky.i: The measure of a theory's content is how much it forbids. A prediction is risky when it could easily have come out otherwise and the theory would have been dead if it had.
risky.x: Einstein predicted a specific angle of light deflection. A different angle would have refuted him outright.
risky.q: Model A predicts GDP growth between 1.9–2.1%; Model B predicts “between −2% and 6%.” Growth is 2.0%. Which passed the riskier test?
risky.a: Model A, assuming the narrow interval was specified in advance and credible rivals allowed wider outcomes. Its success excludes far more possibilities.

adhoc.w: Duhem–Quine makes auxiliary adjustment logically unavoidable: when a prediction fails, something in the bundle must change. The epistemic problem is distinguishing legitimate model improvement from an immunizing patch that explains only the failure already seen. Ad hocness names that failure mode.
adhoc.i: A theory is hit by a disconfirming result. Its defenders add an assumption that accounts for the failure, has no independent support, and generates no new testable predictions. The theory survives — and has become less scientific in the process. Popper called these immunizing stratagems. They are not always illegitimate: auxiliary assumptions get adjusted all the time in healthy science. The test is what the adjustment buys you.
adhoc.x: “The effect is real but was masked by an unmeasured factor” — offered with no way to identify or measure the factor.
adhoc.q: After a failed prediction, a team adds an unobserved factor calibrated exactly to restore the fit and makes no new prediction. What would change the diagnosis from ad hoc rescue to progressive refinement?
adhoc.a: Independent empirical consequences: a way to measure the factor, a novel prediction it generates, or a new constraint it passes that was not used in constructing the rescue.

corrob.w: Popper wants science without induction. If past success raised the probability that a universal theory will continue to succeed, induction would have returned. So he sharply restricts “corroborated” to a historical appraisal: the theory has faced risky tests and not yet failed. That licenses preference in inquiry, but not the claim that the theory is probably true.
corrob.i: A theory that has survived severe testing is corroborated. Popper insists this does not make it probable, or supported, or more likely to hold next time. It means only that it has not been refuted yet.
corrob.x: A thousand successful tests still do not establish the next case. The logic has not changed since the first test.
corrob.q: A theory has survived ten severe, pre-specified tests. What can a strict Popperian say—and what can they not say?
corrob.a: They can say it is highly corroborated relative to rivals and has survived serious criticism. They cannot infer from that alone that the theory is probably true or that the eleventh test is likely to succeed.

duhem.w: Popper's method needs a clean refutation: predict X, observe not-X, discard the theory. Duhem noticed that this never happens in a laboratory. The prediction was derived from the hypothesis plus assumptions about the instrument, the sample, the background theory, and the absence of interference. Logic condemns the conjunction, not any particular conjunct.
duhem.i: Suppose a telescope fails to show the predicted stellar parallax. The candidate culprits are: the astronomical theory, the optics of the lens, the assumed distance to the star, atmospheric conditions, the observer's competence, and the auxiliary claim that nothing else interferes. The observation refutes their conjunction. It says nothing about which member to abandon. Quine radicalised this into confirmation holism: our beliefs face experience as a corporate body, and any statement can be held true come what may if we make drastic enough adjustments elsewhere in the system. Even logic and mathematics are, in principle, revisable.
duhem.x: The telescope disconfirms the prediction. Is the theory wrong, or the lens, or the atmosphere, or the observer?
duhem.q: Your specification produces a null result on an effect you expected. List the bundle before you conclude anything. What is on it?
duhem.a: At minimum: the causal hypothesis itself; the functional form; the identification strategy's assumptions; the measurement validity of your proxies; the sample's representativeness; the time period's regime stability; and the power of the test to detect an effect of that size. The null condemns the conjunction. Reporting it as evidence against the hypothesis alone is a claim about which member you have independently ruled out — and that claim needs its own defence.

underdet.w: Even perfect handling of a dataset may leave rival explanations tied. This matters because scientific inference often asks more than “which theory fits?”—it asks which unobserved structure, mechanism, or counterfactual is real. When several rivals fit the total evidence, extra theoretical virtues or new experiments must do the separating.
underdet.i: For any finite body of evidence, more than one theory fits it. Data alone never uniquely picks out a theory, so something besides data always completes the choice.
underdet.x: Several specifications fit the same series equally well and imply materially different policies.
underdet.q: Three structural models reproduce every observable moment in your dataset but imply different policy counterfactuals. What does better standard error precision on those moments solve?
underdet.a: It may solve sampling uncertainty but not the structural underdetermination. You need new identifying variation, restrictions, experiments, or defensible theoretical assumptions that separate the observationally equivalent models.

kuhn.w: Popper’s picture suggests scientists constantly try to refute theories. Kuhn’s history showed something else: mature science spends long periods solving puzzles inside a framework and tolerating anomalies. The paradigm concept explains how a community can rationally work within a protected structure until accumulated strain produces crisis.
kuhn.i: Kuhn's history shows science does not accumulate smoothly. It works for long stretches inside a shared framework — a paradigm — solving puzzles the framework defines and treating anomalies as unsolved puzzles rather than as refutations. Anomalies accumulate. Eventually a crisis develops, a rival framework appears, and the community switches. The switch is not a simple matter of evidence, because the two frameworks disagree about what counts as evidence.
kuhn.x: Ptolemaic astronomy was not stupid. It was a functioning paradigm that absorbed anomalies for centuries before it broke.
kuhn.q: A field keeps its core framework despite recurring anomalies because it continues solving new puzzles and training researchers successfully. Is that automatically irrational on Kuhn’s account?
kuhn.a: No. That is normal science. Anomalies are expected and need not trigger abandonment until they become severe, persistent, and connected to a viable alternative framework.

normal.w: Popper’s image makes scientists look like permanent revolutionaries trying to refute their own theories. Kuhn’s history showed that productive research usually does the opposite: it treats core commitments as fixed enough to define solvable puzzles. Without that temporary dogmatism, cumulative technical work would be impossible.
normal.i: The ordinary condition of research: solving puzzles inside an accepted framework, not testing the framework. Most scientific work, most of the time, is this.
normal.x: Refining an estimate within an accepted model rather than asking whether the model should be the model.
normal.q: You spend months refining a parameter estimate inside an accepted model and never ask whether that model family is right. In Kuhn’s vocabulary, what are you doing?
normal.a: Normal science: solving a puzzle defined by the paradigm. That is not a criticism unless the framework is in crisis and the deeper assumptions are precisely what need examination.

incomm.w: If paradigms merely made competing predictions in a fixed vocabulary, evidence could rank them on one common scale. Kuhn and Feyerabend argue revolutionary change can alter the meanings of terms and the standards of good explanation themselves, making comparison real but not algorithmically neutral.
incomm.i: Rival paradigms may share no common measure. Key terms shift meaning across the divide, so the theories cannot be compared claim by claim in a neutral vocabulary.
incomm.x: “Mass” does not mean the same thing in Newtonian and relativistic physics, so the two theories are not making rival claims about one shared quantity.
incomm.q: Two models use the same word “risk” but one defines it as variance and the other as expected shortfall. Before comparing empirical claims, what incommensurability-style task comes first?
incomm.a: Align the concepts and inferential roles. Apparent disagreement may partly reflect a change in what the central term measures; comparison requires translation before scorekeeping.

theoryladen.w: Scientific arguments often imagine a clean division between neutral observation and interpretation. Theory-ladenness complicates that picture: what is noticed, measured, classified, and even described can depend on prior theoretical commitments. This matters most when rival theories help construct the evidence used to choose between them.
theoryladen.i: What counts as data, and how it is described, already depends on theoretical commitments. There is no neutral observation language waiting underneath.
theoryladen.x: Two economists look at the same series and see different things, because they are looking for different variables.
theoryladen.q: Two teams receive the same transaction log but construct different “liquidity events” because their theories define the category differently. Where is the theory-ladenness?
theoryladen.a: In the transformation from record to observation category. The underlying log may be shared, but what counts as an instance of the measured phenomenon depends on conceptual and coding commitments.

lakatos.w: Popper said refutation kills theories. Kuhn showed historically that it does not, and that scientists are right to protect a framework while it is still productive. That left a gap: if anomalies do not force abandonment, what distinguishes legitimate protection from mere stubbornness? Lakatos's programme concept is the answer, and it is the most usable idea in the philosophy of science.
lakatos.i: A research programme has a hard core — the commitments its adherents will not give up — surrounded by a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses, initial conditions, and observational assumptions. Anomalies are directed at the belt, never at the core. That is not cheating; it is how every functioning science operates. The evaluation is therefore historical rather than logical. Ask what the belt adjustments accomplished. If they generated predictions of novel facts that were subsequently confirmed, the programme is progressive. If they merely accommodated the anomaly that prompted them, adding no new content, it is degenerating.
lakatos.x: Adding epicycles that explain nothing new is degenerating. Predicting Neptune from anomalies in Uranus's orbit is progressive — same manoeuvre, opposite verdict.
lakatos.q: Two macro schools each explain the last recession after the fact. How would Lakatos tell them apart?
lakatos.a: Not by which explanation fits better — both fit, that is what post-hoc explanation does. He would ask what each school predicted in advance that it did not already know, and whether those predictions were confirmed. A school whose adjustments have generated confirmed novel predictions is progressive; a school whose adjustments only ever explain the last crisis after it happens is degenerating, however elegant the explanation.

expl.w: Prediction and explanation can come apart. Hempel’s deductive-nomological model captured one ideal: derive the event from laws plus conditions. Counterexamples showed that derivability alone misses direction and relevance; the height of a flagpole explains its shadow, but the shadow length does not symmetrically explain the height. Later accounts emphasize causes, mechanisms, or unification.
expl.i: What makes something an explanation rather than a description? Hempel's answer: derive the phenomenon from a general law plus initial conditions. Later accounts appeal to causal mechanisms or to unification instead.
expl.x: The flagpole's height explains the shadow's length. The shadow's length does not explain the height — although the derivation runs both ways.
expl.q: A model forecasts defaults well because it uses a proxy tightly correlated with distress, but the proxy has no stable causal relation. Does forecasting success establish explanation?
expl.a: No. It establishes predictive usefulness under the observed regime. Explanation requires an account of why the relation holds and whether it would survive interventions or changes in the data-generating process.

ibe.w: Much reasoning is neither deduction nor simple enumeration. From footprints you infer a walker; from a pattern of prices you infer a mechanism. Abduction/IBE formalizes the move from evidence to explanatory hypothesis and makes explicit the extra virtues—simplicity, scope, mechanism, unification—used to choose among compatible accounts.
ibe.i: Infer the hypothesis that would best explain the evidence, where “best” draws on simplicity, scope, and unifying power. Most real reasoning outside mathematics has this shape.
ibe.x: Footprints in fresh snow. Someone walked here. You did not deduce it and you did not generalise from a sample.
ibe.q: A model explains an anomaly elegantly, but you never compared it with two obvious rival mechanisms. What is the IBE failure?
ibe.a: You have at most inference to the best explanation in an impoverished comparison set. The “best” judgment is only as strong as the alternative search; the bad-lot problem remains.

realism.w: The dispute decides what scientific success entitles us to believe. Realists use novel prediction, explanation, and intervention to argue that electrons, genes, fields, or latent mechanisms are not merely useful fictions. Anti-realists point to underdetermination and historical theory change to argue that empirical success can be retained without literal belief in the full ontology.
realism.i: Does a successful theory describe unobservable reality, or is it only a reliable instrument for organising and predicting observations?
realism.x: Do electrons exist, or is “electron” an extremely useful bookkeeping device?
realism.q: A model predicts extremely well out of sample. What extra step does a realist take that a constructive empiricist need not?
realism.a: The realist treats that success as evidence that at least some unobservable structure posited by the model is approximately true; the constructive empiricist can accept the predictions while remaining agnostic about that ontology.

miracle.w: Realists argue that if a theory’s hidden structure bore no relation to reality, repeated precise success—especially on phenomena not used to construct it—would be an astonishing coincidence. Approximate truth is offered as the explanation that makes scientific success unsurprising.
miracle.i: The predictive success of science would be a miracle if its theories were not at least approximately true. Realism is offered as the only non-miraculous explanation of that success.
miracle.q: Which kind of empirical success gives the no-miracles argument its strongest force?
miracle.a: Novel, risky, precise success on phenomena not used to build or tune the theory—especially when rival theories did not predict the same outcome.

pmi.w: Scientific realism often points to success: surely it would be miraculous for radically false theories to predict so well. Laudan turns history against that inference. The record contains theories that were successful enough for their time yet posited entities or mechanisms later abandoned. Success may therefore outrun truth.
pmi.i: Past theories were predictively successful and turned out false. By induction, our current successful theories are probably false too.
pmi.x: Phlogiston, caloric, the luminiferous ether. Each worked, each was abandoned.
pmi.q: What must a selective realist show to answer the pessimistic meta-induction convincingly?
pmi.a: They must identify, by a principled rule, which components of successful theories are responsible for success and tend to survive theory change—not merely label the survivors “approximately true” afterward.

constemp.w: Scientific theories often posit entities and structures far beyond direct observation. Realism says predictive success is evidence those posits are approximately true; constructive empiricism offers a disciplined alternative: use the theory and believe what it says about observables while remaining agnostic about unobservables. This preserves scientific practice without the extra metaphysical commitment.
constemp.i: The aim of science is empirical adequacy — getting the observable phenomena right — not truth about unobservables. Accepting a theory means using it, not believing everything it posits.
constemp.q: You rely heavily on a model’s latent states for prediction but refuse to say those states literally exist in the world. Which stance is this closest to?
constemp.a: Constructive empiricism or a nearby anti-realist stance: accept the model for its empirical adequacy while withholding belief in the literal ontology of the unobservables.

causal.w: Data can reveal patterns of co-movement without telling us which variables would change if we actively changed another. Confounding, selection, reverse causation, and measurement can produce the same associations. Modern causal inference makes the extra assumptions explicit—through DAGs, potential outcomes, instruments, natural experiments, or structural models—so the inferential leap can be inspected rather than hidden.
causal.i: When is a correlation entitled to a causal reading? This is the most technically developed part of modern philosophy of science, and the part where philosophy and working method have genuinely fused. The central insight is that causal conclusions require causal assumptions. No amount of purely observational data yields a causal claim on its own — the assumptions have to come from somewhere outside the dataset, and the honest move is to write them down.
causal.x: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together every summer. Neither causes the other, and no statistic in the dataset says so.
causal.q: Your regression coefficient is precisely estimated and robust to many specifications. What is still missing before it earns a causal interpretation?
causal.a: An identification argument: why, under explicit causal assumptions, the observed variation corresponds to the intervention or counterfactual quantity of interest rather than confounding, selection, reverse causation, or another path.

ladder.w: The ladder is a compact diagnostic for overclaiming. Rung one asks what is associated with what; rung two asks what happens if we do X; rung three asks what would have happened to this unit had X been different. Moving upward changes the question, not merely the statistical sophistication of the answer.
ladder.i: Three rungs: association (seeing), intervention (doing), and counterfactuals (imagining what would have been). Questions on a higher rung cannot be answered with data from a lower one.
ladder.x: Correlation tells you what accompanies what. Only intervention tells you what happens if you change it.
ladder.q: “People who receive the program do better” is rung one. What change turns the question into rung two?
ladder.a: Ask what outcomes would occur if eligible people were assigned or caused to receive the program—the intervention question, not merely the observed association among recipients.

confound.w: Regression does not know which variables are confounders. The decision requires a causal model. DAGs make assumed paths explicit so analysts can distinguish variables that should be adjusted for from mediators, colliders, and irrelevant predictors. “Control for everything” is not conservative—it can create bias.
confound.i: A common cause of both treatment and outcome produces association without causation. Directed acyclic graphs make the assumed causal structure explicit so the required adjustments can be derived rather than guessed.
confound.x: Wealth causes both private schooling and later earnings, so the raw association between the two overstates the effect of schooling.
confound.q: Wealth affects both private-school attendance and adult earnings. What role does wealth play in the raw schooling–earnings association?
confound.a: A confounder/common cause. Failing to address the backdoor path through wealth can make the schooling association look more causal than it is.

collider.w: Collider bias is dangerous because it often enters through apparently careful sample restriction or “controlling.” If admission depends on grades and test scores, then among admitted students a low value on one must be compensated by a high value on the other, inducing a negative relation even when none exists in the applicant population.
collider.i: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables induces a spurious association between them. This is the error sophisticated analysts make, because it looks like careful controlling.
collider.x: Among admitted students, test scores and grades correlate negatively — because either one alone could have won admission.
collider.q: In a dataset containing only firms that survived a crisis, resilience practices and balance-sheet strength are negatively associated. What should you suspect before interpreting the tradeoff?
collider.a: Survival may be a collider caused by both practices and balance-sheet strength. Conditioning on survivors can induce a negative association even if the two factors were independent in the full population.

simpson.w: The paradox demonstrates that “the data” do not dictate one aggregation level. A treatment can outperform in every subgroup yet look worse overall if treatment groups contain different mixes of high- and low-risk cases. Both arithmetic summaries can be correct; deciding which is relevant requires the causal question.
simpson.i: A trend present in every subgroup can reverse when the subgroups are combined. Both the aggregated and disaggregated numbers are correct; they answer different questions.
simpson.x: A treatment better for men and better for women, yet worse for people overall.
simpson.q: A treatment is better for men and better for women but worse overall. What must you inspect before deciding which conclusion matters?
simpson.a: The group composition and causal role of sex in assignment/outcome, plus the estimand of interest. The reversal itself does not tell you whether to aggregate or stratify.

values.w: Rudner’s point is not that facts are political. It is that acceptance under uncertainty embeds a loss function. False positives and false negatives have different costs, so choosing a threshold cannot be determined by likelihood alone. Heather Douglas’s work on inductive risk develops how social and ethical values legitimately enter decisions about evidential standards without dictating the evidence itself.
values.i: Rudner's argument: since no hypothesis is ever conclusively verified, accepting one always means deciding that the evidence is sufficient. How much is sufficient depends on how bad the two kinds of error would be. That is a value judgment, and it cannot be delegated to the statistics. Heather Douglas developed this into the modern literature on inductive risk. The upshot is not that science is political; it is that the value judgment is unavoidable, and therefore should be made explicitly and by the right people.
values.x: Setting α = 0.05 in a drug trial is a decision about how many deaths of each kind you are willing to tolerate. Nothing in the mathematics tells you where to put it.
values.q: Two regulators agree on the evidence but choose different evidentiary thresholds because one prioritizes avoiding false negatives and the other false positives. Is that necessarily scientific disagreement?
values.a: No. It may be a disagreement about inductive risk and the relative costs of error. The scientific evidence can be shared while the acceptance threshold reflects different values.

repl.w: Failure to reproduce famous results exposed a structural rather than merely individual problem. Low power, publication bias, flexible analysis, weak measurement, small samples, and novelty incentives can generate a literature where many “successful” papers are expected to fail independent repetition. Replication changes the prior on isolated claims and motivates institutional reform.
repl.i: A large share of published findings fail when independently repeated. The causes are mostly structural — incentives, flexible analysis, selective publication — rather than fraudulent.
repl.x: Whole subfields of psychology and medicine failed systematic replication attempts, including results taught as settled.
repl.q: A surprising single-study finding has p=0.02 but no preregistration, low power, and no independent replication. How should the replication crisis affect your prior?
repl.a: It should materially lower confidence relative to the headline result. The relevant base rate includes selective publication and analytic flexibility; independent, well-powered replication should carry much more weight.

pval.w: The most common statistical misreading reverses the conditioning. P(data or more extreme | null) is not P(null | data). A p-value also says nothing by itself about effect size, practical importance, study design, multiple analyses, or prior plausibility. The concept matters because precise language limits what a findings section is entitled to claim.
pval.i: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme given that the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability the result will replicate, and not a measure of effect size or importance.
pval.x: p = 0.04 does not mean a 96% chance the effect is real. It means the data would be unusual if there were no effect.
pval.q: A result has p=0.04. What is the safest short interpretation?
pval.a: Under the specified null model and analysis procedure, data at least this extreme would occur with about 4% probability. It does not by itself give the probability the null is true or the effect will replicate.

forking.w: Classical p-values assume the analysis rule was fixed independently of the realized data. In practice, researchers decide exclusions, transformations, outcomes, interactions, covariates, and stopping rules after seeing partial patterns. The chosen path may look innocent, but the counterfactual set of paths means the nominal error rate no longer describes the procedure actually used.
forking.i: Even with no intent to cheat, analysts make defensible choices that depend on how the data happened to look. The test was therefore never truly pre-specified, and the false positive rate is far above the nominal one.
forking.x: You would have excluded different outliers if the data had looked different. That counterfactual is enough to break the test.
forking.q: You would have used a log transform if the raw outcome had looked more skewed, but it did not, so you report the raw analysis. Why can that still affect inference?
forking.a: Because the analysis rule depended on the observed data. The counterfactual branch is part of the procedure, so the nominal p-value for a fixed raw analysis does not fully describe the selection process.

pubbias.w: Even if every individual study is honestly run, selective visibility can make a weak or nonexistent effect look robust. The epistemic unit is therefore not just the published paper but the process deciding which completed studies become observable. File drawers, selective outcomes, and journal incentives distort apparent replication rates and effect sizes.
pubbias.i: Null results are less likely to be written up and less likely to be accepted, so the published literature systematically over-represents positive findings.
pubbias.x: Twenty studies run, two reach significance, two get published. The literature shows a 100% success rate.
pubbias.q: Twenty teams test an effect; two get p<0.05 and publish, eighteen null studies disappear. What does the published literature falsely suggest?
pubbias.a: A 100% visible success rate and inflated evidence for the effect, even though the pattern is exactly what chance could generate under selective publication.

social.w: Most knowledge is socially acquired, so an epistemology of isolated individuals misses the dominant information channel. The central task is to distinguish genuine distributed evidence from copied consensus and to design institutions that aggregate information rather than suppress, distort, or duplicate it.
social.i: Traditional epistemology studied a lone knower with evidence in front of them. That picture describes almost none of your actual epistemic life. Nearly everything you believe arrived through other people, institutions, and systems for producing and certifying claims. Social epistemology studies the effects of that: when to trust testimony, how a non-expert can evaluate experts, what to do when a peer disagrees, and how groups can be collectively worse than their members. This is where most real-world epistemic failure actually happens, and it is the branch practitioners study least.
social.x: You have never verified the boiling point of mercury, the population of Brazil, or the safety of the building you are sitting in.
social.q: A committee has ten unanimous experts but all were trained by the same lab, use the same dataset, and cite the same paper. What social-epistemic question dominates the headcount?
social.a: Independence. The apparent ten votes may represent one evidential lineage. You should trace source genealogy, method diversity, incentives, and whether any member brings genuinely independent information.

expert.w: Modern knowledge is specialized. On most technical questions, a novice cannot directly evaluate the core evidence without becoming an expert. Social epistemology therefore needs second-order criteria for deciding whom to trust when qualified people disagree or when credentials alone are not enough.
expert.i: Goldman's question: when two experts disagree and you cannot assess the substance, what can a novice legitimately go on? He gives five criteria. The quality of the arguments each presents. The agreement of other experts. Independent evidence that each is genuinely expert. Interests and biases that might distort them. And their track record of past claims that later resolved. The last is by far the hardest to fake and by far the least often checked.
expert.x: Two economists disagree about a policy. You cannot referee the models — but you can check whether either has ever made a dated, checkable prediction.
expert.q: Two PhDs disagree on a specialized issue you cannot technically referee. One publishes transparent forecasts with a good dated record; the other has a stronger title but no checkable history. Which Goldman-style evidence favors the first?
expert.a: Track record and independently assessable performance. Titles still matter as evidence of training, but when direct evaluation is unavailable a public record of successful, checkable judgments is powerful second-order evidence.

disag.w: Disagreement can itself be evidence that your reasoning went wrong. But if you always defer, rational inquiry becomes unstable; if you never move, the existence of an equally competent dissenter has no epistemic effect. The debate asks how to update on another mind as evidence.
disag.i: An epistemic peer — someone equally informed and equally capable — reaches the opposite conclusion from the same evidence. Conciliationism says you should move substantially toward them. The steadfast view says you may hold your position.
disag.x: You and an equally competent colleague read the same file and reach opposite conclusions. Should either of you move?
disag.q: You and a colleague with a historically similar forecast record independently analyze the same evidence and reach 80% versus 20%. What should happen before either says “I’m just more confident”?
disag.a: Treat the disagreement as higher-order evidence and investigate whether the peer and independence assumptions hold. If they do, both should normally move toward less extreme credences; how far is the substantive conciliation debate.

aumann.w: Persistent disagreement feels normal, but the theorem reveals how much hidden asymmetry it requires. If two perfectly rational Bayesian agents begin from the same prior and each knows the other’s posterior, and knows that the other knows, and so on, their posteriors must coincide. Real disagreement therefore diagnoses failure of at least one idealizing condition.
aumann.i: Two rational agents with common priors, who each know the other's posterior, cannot agree to disagree. Persistent disagreement between them is formally impossible.
aumann.x: Formally proven, and almost never observed. Which tells you at least one condition fails in every real disagreement.
aumann.q: Two Bayesian analysts publicly know each other’s posterior but continue to disagree. What does the theorem tell you to look for rather than simply calling one irrational?
aumann.a: A failed assumption: different priors, private information not fully revealed, lack of common knowledge, different models, non-Bayesian updating, or strategic reporting. Persistent disagreement identifies a wedge.

echo.w: The standard diagnosis of political and professional polarisation is that people are not hearing the other side, and the standard prescription follows: expose them to it. That prescription frequently fails and sometimes backfires. Nguyen's argument is that we have been treating two structurally different phenomena as one, and the remedy for each is close to the opposite of the remedy for the other.
echo.i: An epistemic bubble is a structure of omission. Through self-selection, algorithmic filtering, or simple social geography, certain voices never reach you. You are not hostile to them; you have not encountered them. Bubbles are fragile — a single serious encounter with a well-informed dissenter can pop one. An echo chamber is a structure of active discrediting. Outside sources are not absent; they have been pre-emptively characterised as biased, corrupt, or captured. The member has heard the other side and has been supplied, in advance, with a reason to dismiss it. The consequence is that an echo chamber is reinforced by contrary evidence.
echo.x: A bubble pops when you meet a dissenter. An echo chamber has already explained why that particular dissenter is compromised.
echo.q: How would you tell, from inside, whether your own field is an echo chamber rather than merely a bubble?
echo.a: Ask whether your field has a standing account of why its usual critics are not worth taking seriously — and then ask whether that account is falsifiable. If there is a ready explanation for why critics from a given direction are motivated, unserious, or captured, and no evidence from that direction could ever survive it, that is the signature. The bubble test is easier: have you actually read the best version of the outside case, or only summaries produced by people inside?

cascade.w: Social agreement can look like overwhelming evidence while being generated by sequential copying. Once early choices become informative enough, later people may ignore their own weak private evidence. The group then produces strong consensus without proportionate evidential depth—and a small shock can reverse the cascade.
cascade.i: Each person acts rationally on the combination of their own private signal and the visible choices of those before them. Once enough people have acted, the public information swamps any individual's private signal, and everyone afterwards rationally ignores what they themselves know. The result is a confident consensus that almost nobody independently verified — reached by a sequence of individually rational steps.
cascade.x: Three experts cite the same original source. The fourth cites the three. By the tenth, the claim has ten citations and one piece of evidence.
cascade.q: Five analysts each see earlier recommendations before issuing their own, and later reports cite the growing consensus rather than private evidence. What should you trace?
cascade.a: The information genealogy. If later choices were driven by earlier public choices, the apparent five-way confirmation may contain only the first few private signals; the rest are socially correlated echoes.

condorcet.w: The Condorcet theorem formalizes why aggregating many modestly competent judgments can outperform a single expert. But its power comes from assumptions that social systems routinely violate—especially independence. Herding, common information, correlated incentives, and shared models can make a thousand votes behave epistemically like one.
condorcet.i: If each voter is even slightly better than chance and votes independently, the probability that the majority is right approaches certainty as the group grows.
condorcet.x: A thousand slightly-better-than-random judges beat one expert. The condition doing all the work is independence.
condorcet.q: One hundred analysts independently receive the same flawed vendor dataset and all reach the same conclusion. Does Condorcet give you strong confidence?
condorcet.a: No. Their judgments are highly correlated through a common error source. The apparent group size is 100, but the effective independent evidential base may be close to one.

injust.w: Knowledge systems can fail before evidence reaches a formal decision rule. Testimonial injustice distorts credibility assignments; hermeneutical injustice distorts what can even be articulated and recognized. The concept therefore locates epistemic failure in social power, not only in individual reasoning.
injust.i: Wrongs done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice: prejudice causes a hearer to give a speaker's word less credit than it deserves. Hermeneutical injustice: a group lacks the shared concepts needed to make sense of its own experience.
injust.x: A complaint dismissed because of who raised it rather than what it said.
injust.q: A recurring operational problem is dismissed because frontline staff lack the accepted vocabulary to describe it in management categories. Which form is closest?
injust.a: Hermeneutical injustice: the interpretive resources available to the institution make the experience difficult to render intelligible, so knowledge is lost before ordinary credibility assessment even begins.

fem.w: Traditional epistemology often models an isolated knower, but real knowledge is produced inside institutions with agendas, divisions of labor, and unequal access. Feminist epistemology asks whether those structures create systematic blind spots and whether greater objectivity can sometimes require including perspectives that dominant inquiry excluded.
fem.i: Studies how social position shapes what gets investigated, who is credited, and which questions are asked at all. Standpoint theory argues some positions afford better access to particular facts, because those in them have had to understand both the system and their place in it.
fem.x: Which effects of a policy get measured depends on who designed the study and what they expected to find.
fem.q: A study team is demographically diverse but all members were trained in the same method, use the same dataset, and answer to the same incentive structure. What question would feminist epistemology still press?
fem.a: Whether the inquiry actually contains diverse epistemic standpoints, criticism, and access to different evidence—not merely demographic variety without methodological or institutional independence.

natur.w: Normative rules are useless if no real mind can implement them, and theories of reasoning should learn from psychology, cognitive science, and behavioral evidence. The central tension is how to use descriptive science without collapsing “how people do think” into “how they should think.”
natur.i: Quine's proposal: stop asking from the armchair how knowledge ought to work and study empirically how it does. Epistemology becomes a chapter of psychology — the study of how sensory input produces theoretical output. This is the doorway through which the entire heuristics-and-biases literature entered philosophy, and it is why a paper about anchoring effects counts as epistemology.
natur.x: Rather than defining justification, measure which processes actually produce true beliefs and under what conditions.
natur.q: A heuristic violates an ideal Bayesian rule in a lab but beats the formal model out of sample in a noisy real environment. What naturalized-epistemology question follows?
natur.a: Which norm is appropriate to the actual task and resource constraints? The empirical success does not automatically make the heuristic rational, but it forces the normative theory to explain why its ideal rule performs worse in the environment of interest.

quine.w: If foundationalist reconstruction cannot derive science from indubitable experience, Quine argues that epistemology should stop trying to stand outside science and instead become part of it. The project shifts from “what ultimate justification is possible?” toward “how does this cognitive system in fact produce its picture of the world from limited input?”
quine.i: Quine's 1969 essay argued the foundationalist project had failed and should be replaced by empirical inquiry into how humans actually get from meagre sensory input to elaborate theory.
quine.q: A study explains exactly why people form a certain belief. What question remains if you reject full Quinean replacement?
quine.a: Whether that belief-forming process is epistemically good—reliable, responsible, evidence-sensitive, or otherwise justified. Causal explanation does not by itself settle normative status.

hb.w: The program transformed reasoning research by showing that errors are systematic rather than random: availability, representativeness, anchoring, conjunction errors, and base-rate neglect can be elicited repeatedly. Its practical value is large, but so is the temptation to turn a catalog of effects into a theory that people are globally irrational.
hb.i: Systematic, predictable departures from normative reasoning: availability, representativeness, anchoring, base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy.
hb.x: People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind — which tracks memorability, not frequency.
hb.q: A classic bias effect disappears when probabilities are restated as natural frequencies. What should you conclude?
hb.a: Not immediately that the participants were irrational or that the bias is fake. The representation format is causally important, so the normative benchmark and task ecology need to be part of the explanation.

conf.w: The danger is not merely noticing supportive evidence. Rational inquiry should seek evidence that discriminates among hypotheses, and often the most informative test is one designed to fail your favored view. Confirmation bias distorts the search process before the final interpretation even begins.
conf.i: The tendency to seek, notice, and weight evidence that supports what you already believe, and to work less hard at finding what would count against it. Wason's 2-4-6 task is the classic demonstration. Participants are given a triple that fits a hidden rule and asked to discover the rule by proposing further triples. Almost everyone proposes triples they expect to fit. Almost nobody proposes one they expect to fail — which is the only kind of test that could disconfirm.
conf.x: You run the specification you expect to work. When it works, you stop. The decision to stop is where the bias lives.
conf.q: You run specifications until the expected sign appears, then stop and report the successful version. Where exactly is the confirmation bias?
conf.a: In the asymmetric search and stopping rule. The reported estimate may be computed correctly, but the process selectively samples the specification space until it produces confirmatory evidence.

motiv.w: Reasoning skill does not guarantee truth-seeking. A capable thinker can use greater cognitive resources to build stronger defenses for a preferred conclusion. The problem is especially important in political, organizational, and identity-laden settings where being right competes with belonging, status, or material incentives.
motiv.i: Reasoning bent by what you want to be true, or by what your group membership commits you to. Distinct from confirmation bias: the distortion serves a goal, not merely a prior.
motiv.x: Kahan's finding: on politicised questions, more numerate people are more polarised, not less. The skill serves the motive.
motiv.q: An analyst applies harsh robustness standards to results that hurt her preferred policy but accepts friendly results after one specification. What evidence would distinguish motivated reasoning from ordinary methodological inconsistency?
motiv.a: A systematic directional asymmetry tied to the preferred conclusion—especially if standards reverse when the policy direction reverses or incentives/identity cues are experimentally changed. One inconsistent choice alone does not establish motive.

ecolog.w: A heuristic that looks suboptimal in a laboratory can outperform a computationally perfect rule when information is scarce, costs matter, and the environment has stable cues. Gigerenzer’s challenge is therefore benchmark-sensitive: rationality may consist in matching a tool to an ecology rather than maximizing under an unrealistic model of unlimited information.
ecolog.i: Gigerenzer's challenge to the heuristics-and-biases programme. Heuristics are not defective shortcuts measured against a logical ideal; they are adaptations fitted to particular environments. Judged against the right benchmark — performance in the world rather than conformity to a formal rule — they often beat optimisation. Many celebrated “biases” also turn out to be artefacts of how the question was posed. Present the same problem in natural frequencies rather than probabilities and the error rate collapses.
ecolog.x: “10 out of every 1,000 women” produces correct answers where “a 1% probability” produces confusion, in the same population.
ecolog.q: A simple rule beats a complex optimizer out of sample because the optimizer overfits noisy inputs. What would ecological rationality emphasize?
ecolog.a: The simple rule may be better matched to the environment’s uncertainty, data limits, and cue structure. Rationality should be judged against performance under those conditions, not complexity alone.

argth.w: It explains an otherwise puzzling pattern: people often exhibit myside bias when reasoning alone yet improve dramatically when genuine disagreement forces them to evaluate opposing reasons. On this view, some “biases” are side effects of a system designed for interactive argument rather than private optimization.
argth.i: Reason did not evolve to help a solitary thinker find truth. It evolved to produce arguments that persuade others and to evaluate the arguments others produce. On that account, confirmation bias is not a bug — it is the design working as intended.
argth.x: People reason poorly alone and markedly better in groups where real disagreement is present.
argth.q: What institutional design follows most directly if the argumentative theory is broadly right?
argth.a: Build genuine adversarial exchange: independent analyses, red teams, and incentives to challenge rather than merely asking each individual to “debias” alone.

blind.w: Bias education can perversely increase confidence: once you can name errors, you become better at diagnosing opponents while assuming your own introspection reveals unbiased motives. The blind spot is therefore a meta-bias—a failure in how we apply the concept of bias itself.
blind.i: People readily recognise bias in others and reliably fail to see it in themselves — including immediately after being taught the list of biases.
blind.x: Learning this material mostly improves your detection of other people's errors. That is the finding, and it applies to you reading it now.
blind.q: You can list three biases in a colleague’s memo but none in your own, because “I know why I reached my conclusion.” What is the correct next move?
blind.a: Do not trust the asymmetry. Apply an externalized audit to your own work: pre-specified alternatives, a decision log, independent replication, or a red team. The blind spot is exactly why introspective innocence is weak evidence.

virtue.w: Rules can be gamed and evidence can be selectively handled. A theory of good inquiry also needs the agent’s competence, motives, and habits. Virtue approaches explain knowledge and responsible inquiry through intellectual abilities or character traits that make truth and understanding more reliably attainable.
virtue.i: Reverse the order of analysis. Instead of assessing beliefs and then asking what kind of person produces good ones, start with the person: their stable dispositions of inquiry, good and bad. Careful attention is a virtue; jumping to conclusions is a vice. Only then assess the beliefs those dispositions produce. The practical consequence is a shift from auditing outputs to auditing habits — which is the only thing that generalises to the next problem.
virtue.x: Assess the inquirer's habits before assessing the conclusion. A good conclusion from bad habits will not repeat.
virtue.q: A researcher gets the answer right through a process she does not understand and cannot reproduce, while another gets it right through a well-calibrated skill. What does virtue epistemology care about?
virtue.a: Whether the truth is attributable to the agent’s epistemic competence or character rather than luck. Successful performance “because of” ability is central, not truth alone.

ivirt.w: Good reasoning depends not only on rules but on the person applying them. An agent can know every fallacy and still avoid threatening evidence, defend status, or stop inquiry early. Virtue epistemology asks what traits make someone systematically better at reaching truth, understanding, and responsible belief over time.
ivirt.i: Stable dispositions that make you a better knower: humility, courage, honesty, thoroughness, perseverance, autonomy, open-mindedness.
ivirt.x: Intellectual humility is calibrated confidence, not diffidence. It is compatible with strong claims strongly defended.
ivirt.q: A researcher is strongly confident, states exactly what evidence would overturn the conclusion, and actively funds a replication designed to fail it. Is strong confidence inconsistent with intellectual humility?
ivirt.a: No. That can be exemplary humility: confidence is high but calibrated, limitations are explicit, and the researcher remains genuinely answerable to possible defeat.

ivice.w: Some failures are not one-off reasoning errors. An organization can repeatedly miss evidence because its members are incurious, defensive, or unwilling to admit uncertainty even when each individual inference is technically competent. Vice epistemology diagnoses the posture that generates recurring epistemic failure.
ivice.i: Dispositions that systematically obstruct knowledge: dogmatism, closed-mindedness, gullibility, wishful thinking, intellectual cowardice, arrogance.
ivice.x: Cassam analyses real intelligence and policy failures as vice rather than error — the individual steps were competent and the posture was wrong.
ivice.q: A team repeatedly suppresses inconvenient sensitivity checks because leadership punishes uncertainty. Is the right diagnosis only “individual closed-mindedness”?
ivice.a: No. The behavior is epistemically vicious, but the causal structure is institutional. A good diagnosis targets both the repeated vice-like practice and the incentives that produce and reward it.

scout.w: Many epistemic failures are not deficits of intelligence but failures of objective function. If reasoning is serving identity, status, or victory, better reasoning skill can make defense stronger. The scout metaphor asks the agent to optimize for accurate representation even when accuracy is personally inconvenient.
scout.i: The soldier's job is to defend territory: to attack opposing claims and protect one's own. The scout's job is to make an accurate map: to find out what is actually there, whether or not the news is welcome. Both are reasoning. The difference is what they are for. Galef's argument is that most of us default to soldier mode without noticing, and that the switch is trainable.
scout.x: A scout wants an accurate map even when the accurate map says the position is bad.
scout.q: You are defending a policy you strongly value and discover evidence that weakens its stated mechanism but not necessarily the value goal. What would a scout do?
scout.a: Update the factual map and separate it from the value commitment: concede the mechanism evidence, revise the instrumental argument, and then ask whether another route serves the same goal. Protecting the value does not require protecting a false empirical story.

clifford.w: The debate separates two dangers: credulity and paralysis. Clifford emphasizes the social and moral costs of training ourselves to believe carelessly; James emphasizes cases where withholding belief is not neutral because the opportunity can disappear or participation helps make the evidence available. The issue generalizes to decisions under irreducible uncertainty.
clifford.i: Clifford's rule is uncompromising: it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence. His case is a shipowner who talks himself into believing his vessel seaworthy. The ship sinks. Clifford's point is that the owner was culpable before it sank — the wrong was in the believing. James replies that for a certain class of choices — live, forced, and momentous, where the evidence cannot decide and not choosing is itself a choice — Clifford's rule is not cautious but paralysing.
clifford.x: You must decide now, the evidence is genuinely indecisive, and declining to decide has consequences of its own. Clifford says withhold; James says that is not available.
clifford.q: A decision must be made tomorrow, the evidence cannot be improved before then, and declining to choose guarantees losing the opportunity. Which side of the Clifford–James debate becomes especially relevant?
clifford.a: James’s. The option may be forced and momentous, so withholding is itself a consequential choice. That does not make any belief true; it changes what commitment may be rationally permissible.

bs.w: Epistemic environments can be damaged not only by false statements but by communication detached from truth-testing altogether. A liar tracks truth closely enough to invert it; the bullshitter optimizes for impression, persuasion, status, or fluency without caring whether the content corresponds to reality.
bs.i: A liar knows the truth and conceals it — and therefore still respects it enough to track it. A bullshitter is indifferent to whether what he says is true. Frankfurt argues the second is the greater enemy of the epistemic commons.
bs.x: Text produced to sound authoritative, with no mechanism anywhere in its production for checking whether it is accurate.
bs.q: A presenter confidently invents a statistic, and later says “great, then use the correct number” with no concern that the original was fabricated. Lie, error, or bullshit?
bs.a: Paradigmatically bullshit: the key feature is indifference to whether the number was true, not necessarily an intention to make the audience believe something the presenter knew was false.

moral.w: Policy arguments routinely combine claims about what will happen with claims about what should matter. Evidence can settle the first while leaving the second untouched. Moral epistemology supplies the vocabulary for that boundary: intuition, reflective equilibrium, moral realism, constructivism, skepticism, and disagreement.
moral.i: How can we know normative claims? By intuition, by a priori reasoning, by reflective equilibrium — adjusting principles and particular judgments against each other until they fit — or not at all, if there are no moral facts to know.
moral.x: Is “this rule is unfair” the kind of claim that can be true, or only the kind that can be shared?
moral.q: Two analysts agree a rule will cost $10 million and prevent one fatality, but disagree whether it should be adopted. What kind of disagreement remains?
moral.a: A normative or moral one about how costs, lives, rights, risk, and institutional duties should be weighted. More empirical precision may help, but it cannot by itself supply the evaluative premise.

logic.w: A dispute can fail even when everyone has the same facts because the inference is invalid, a premise is false, a warrant is hidden, or the burden is assigned differently. Argument analysis makes those layers visible instead of treating disagreement as a collision of conclusions.
logic.i: The machinery of inference, and the diagnostic vocabulary for what is going wrong in a conversation. Formal logic tells you what follows from what. Informal logic tells you why an argument that follows perfectly well can still be worthless — and why one that is technically invalid can still be persuasive and even reasonable. For anyone who argues professionally this is the most immediately usable branch on the map.
logic.x: The question is rarely “is the conclusion true?” It is “does it follow, from what, and on what unstated principle?”
logic.q: Two people agree that a study found X but disagree whether X supports regulation Y. What Toulmin-style question should you ask before collecting more data?
logic.a: “What has to be true for X to support Y?” That exposes the warrant—often the actual location of disagreement—before adding more grounds that both sides may interpret differently.

valid.w: Arguments fail in two fundamentally different places: the inferential bridge can be invalid, or the bridge can be valid while resting on false premises. Separating validity from soundness prevents a common conversational error—attacking a conclusion because one argument for it is bad, or praising an argument because its conclusion happens to be true.
valid.i: An argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises. It is sound if it is valid and the premises are also true. Validity is about structure; soundness adds a claim about the world.
valid.x: Valid but unsound: all fish fly; salmon are fish; therefore salmon fly. The reasoning is impeccable.
valid.q: “All heavily regulated firms fail; Bank X is heavily regulated; therefore Bank X will fail.” The form is valid, but the first premise is false. What is the exact diagnosis?
valid.a: Valid but unsound. The inferential structure transmits the premises correctly, but the argument does not establish the conclusion because at least one premise is false.

modus.w: These two forms are the backbone of deductive testing. They matter because empirical arguments often imitate them without actually satisfying their premises. Popperian falsification has the form of modus tollens only if the prediction really follows from the theory-plus-auxiliaries; otherwise “not Q” does not isolate the theory.
modus.i: Ponens: if P then Q; P; therefore Q. Tollens: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Both are valid. Tollens is the logical form of falsification.
modus.x: If the theory holds we would observe X. We do not observe X. So the theory does not hold.
modus.q: If a theory plus auxiliaries entails X, and X is reliably not observed, what does modus tollens strictly license?
modus.a: It licenses rejection of the conjunction that entailed X. Additional argument is required to decide whether the core theory, an auxiliary, the measurement, or an initial condition should be abandoned.

affirm.w: Empirical reasoning constantly moves from “if the hypothesis is true, we should see Q” to “we see Q.” The temptation is to conclude the hypothesis is true. That move is invalid unless rival explanations of Q are also considered. The concept exists to separate prediction from discrimination: evidence matters only when it is more expected under your hypothesis than under alternatives.
affirm.i: If P then Q; Q; therefore P. This is invalid, and it is the single most common error in empirical reasoning — because it looks exactly like confirmation. The reason it fails is that Q may follow from other things besides P. Observing Q raises P's probability only to the extent that Q is less likely under the alternatives.
affirm.x: If the model is correct we would see this pattern. We see it. Therefore the model is correct. No — three rival models predict the same pattern.
affirm.q: A model predicts spreads will widen during stress. They widen. What must you know before saying this strongly confirms the model?
affirm.a: How likely the widening was under serious rival models. If they also predicted it, the observation has little discriminating force; if they predicted stability, the evidence is much stronger.

toulmin.w: Formal logic represents arguments as premises and a conclusion, which is accurate for mathematics and nearly useless for everything else. Toulmin's complaint was that this apparatus cannot represent the arguments people actually make in law, policy, or science, and so cannot diagnose why they fail. He built a model that can.
toulmin.i: The six parts: the claim you are advancing; the grounds — the data or facts you offer; the warrant, a general principle licensing the step from grounds to claim; the backing that supports the warrant itself; a qualifier indicating strength ('probably', 'in most cases'); and the rebuttal conditions under which the claim would not hold. The warrant is the load-bearing element and it is nearly always implicit, because stating it feels pedantic to the person making the argument. It is also, nine times out of ten, exactly where the disagreement lives.
toulmin.x: Grounds: unemployment rose. Claim: the policy failed. Warrant: unemployment is the right measure of this policy's success. Nobody stated the warrant, and it is the only thing in dispute.
toulmin.q: “Compliance costs rose 12% after the rule, so the rule was too burdensome.” Diagram it. Where is the real dispute?
toulmin.a: Claim: the rule was too burdensome. Grounds: costs rose 12%. Warrant, unstated: a 12% cost increase exceeds the benefit, or cost increases are themselves the measure of burden regardless of benefit. That warrant is the whole argument, and it is doing all the work while nobody examines it. Note also the missing qualifier and rebuttal — no acknowledgement of what else could have raised costs in that period. Attacking the 12% is the obvious move and the wrong one; the number is probably right.

straw.w: Arguments are only informative if they engage the view someone actually holds. Distortion can be deliberate, but more often it comes from compressing a complex claim into a version that is easier to criticize. The remedy is procedural rather than psychological: reconstruct first, obtain agreement on the reconstruction, then object.
straw.i: Refuting a weakened or distorted version of the opponent's position rather than the position they actually hold.
straw.x: “You want more oversight” becomes “you want to shut the industry down”.
straw.q: Before criticizing a colleague’s policy position, what single procedure most reliably prevents a straw man?
straw.a: Restate the position—including its strongest qualifications and warrant—until the colleague agrees that the reconstruction is fair; then attack that version.

motte.w: Some positions survive criticism not because one claim is well defended, but because two claims are traded back and forth. The broad “bailey” does the rhetorical or policy work; under pressure the speaker retreats to the narrow “motte,” wins agreement, and later acts as if the stronger claim was vindicated. The concept exists to freeze the target of evaluation.
motte.i: Named after a medieval fortification: a comfortable but indefensible field (the bailey) beside a fortified mound (the motte) you retreat into when attacked. The move: advance a strong, interesting, contestable claim. When challenged, retreat to a weak, obvious, unobjectionable version and defend that. Once the challenge passes, resume operating on the strong claim as though it had been established.
motte.x: “X is entirely socially constructed” → challenged → “I only mean context matters” → agreed → and later the strong claim is back in use.
motte.q: A speaker says “the model is useless,” retreats under challenge to “the model has important limitations,” then later cites the exchange as proof it should be discarded. What is the move?
motte.a: Motte-and-bailey. “Has important limitations” is the defensible motte; “is useless” is the stronger bailey doing the decision work.

equiv.w: Many disagreements survive because both sides keep using the same label while attaching different criteria to it. The argument then looks valid on paper because the repeated word hides the switch. Naming equivocation gives you a procedural cure: replace the contested word with explicit descriptions and see whether the inference still works.
equiv.i: Using a key term in two different senses at different points in the same argument, so that a valid-looking structure conceals a change of subject.
equiv.x: “Risk” as variance in one premise and as probability of loss in the next. The argument is now about two different things.
equiv.q: A memo says an event is “unlikely” meaning below 5%, then concludes it is “unlikely to matter” meaning economically small. What happened?
equiv.a: Equivocation. The same word moved from probability to magnitude. The second claim needs a separate premise connecting low probability to low expected impact.

authority.w: No individual can independently verify more than a tiny fraction of what they know, so deference is unavoidable. The useful question is not “did someone cite an authority?” but whether this source is epistemically entitled to deference on this proposition. Domain fit, expert consensus, incentives, track record, and independent indicators of competence do the real work.
authority.i: A fallacy when the authority is outside their domain, when the question is genuinely contested among experts, or when the authority's interest is engaged. Perfectly good evidence otherwise.
authority.x: A physicist on climate physics is evidence. The same physicist on monetary policy is not.
authority.q: A Nobel-winning physicist gives a confident view on monetary transmission. What should their Nobel change in your evidential weighting?
authority.a: Very little by itself. It is strong evidence of expertise in physics, not monetary economics. Look for domain-relevant competence, arguments, track record, and agreement among appropriate experts.

burden.w: Many disputes are decided before evidence is weighed because the parties silently assign different defaults. Must a regulator prove a new rule beneficial, or must opponents prove it harmful? Must a claimant establish causation, or must the skeptic produce an alternative? Burden allocation is epistemology turned into procedure.
burden.i: Who must make the case, and who may simply wait? The allocation is rarely obvious, it is usually contested, and it frequently decides the outcome before any evidence is weighed.
burden.x: Must a new rule be shown to be beneficial, or must objectors show it is harmful? The answer decides most of the argument in advance.
burden.q: A policy debate stalls because one side says “show the rule helps” and the other says “show the rule harms.” What is the first epistemic issue to resolve?
burden.a: The burden and default: which state persists under unresolved uncertainty, what evidence threshold changes it, and why the costs of error justify that allocation. Without that, the parties are not yet weighing evidence under the same decision rule.

steel.w: The easiest argument to defeat is rarely the one worth defeating. Steelmanning exists as a discipline against selection bias in criticism: if you choose the weakest formulation, you learn almost nothing about whether the core position survives. A strong reconstruction also exposes the real crux, because superficial wording differences have already been repaired.
steel.i: Engage the strongest version of the opposing view — including improvements its own advocates have not thought of. Rapoport's rule: restate the position so well that your opponent says they wish they had put it that way.
steel.x: If your summary of their view would embarrass them, you are arguing with something they do not believe.
steel.q: What is the best sign that you have steelmanned rather than merely paraphrased an opposing view?
steel.a: The advocate recognizes the thesis, but the supporting warrant or evidence is stronger, clearer, and harder to attack than in the original presentation.

relig.w: Religious claims sit where ordinary evidential standards, existential commitment, testimony, metaphysics, and identity meet. The point of the branch is not to decide theology in advance but to ask which epistemic rules apply: Clifford versus James, Plantinga’s proper basicality, fideism, hinge approaches, and Flew’s challenge about immunization.
relig.i: Whether and how religious belief can be rational. This is the richest cross-connection on the map, because it sits at the junction of three branches: the structure of justification, the epistemology of testimony, and the ethics of belief. It is also the best available test case. Positions about foundations that sound abstract become concrete the moment they are applied to something people actually care about, and their costs become visible.
relig.x: Is faith a conclusion drawn from evidence, a properly basic belief needing none, or something not in the justification business at all? Three different branches, three different answers.
relig.q: A religious claim is said to be properly basic, but a critic asks why an incompatible tradition cannot say exactly the same. What epistemic problem has appeared?
relig.a: The symmetry/Great-Pumpkin problem: the theory needs a principled account of proper basicality, cognitive conditions, and defeaters that distinguishes warranted basic belief from arbitrary exemption.

evidfid.w: Religious belief concentrates the general problem of whether every rational commitment must be proportioned to evidence of the usual kind. The evidentialist worries that exempting faith licenses arbitrary belief; the fideist worries that demanding prior proof misunderstands the role of trust, commitment, or a form of life.
evidfid.i: Evidentialism holds religious belief to the same evidential standard as any other. Fideism holds that faith is not the kind of thing evidence governs, and that demanding evidence misunderstands what is being claimed.
evidfid.q: Someone says, “This belief is faith, so no possible evidence could count against it.” What is the epistemic danger?
evidfid.a: The claim turns fideism into complete immunization. A defensible non-evidential stance still needs to explain boundaries and defeaters; otherwise any arbitrary belief can claim the same exemption.

reformed.w: If some ordinary beliefs—memory, other minds, the external world—are rational without being inferred from proofs, religious belief may not be uniquely required to pass an evidential argument first. Reformed epistemology uses foundationalism to challenge the assumption that rational theism must be a conclusion.
reformed.i: Plantinga's argument: belief in God can be properly basic — foundational rather than inferred — and therefore rational without any supporting argument at all. The move is structural, not devotional. Plantinga points out that belief in other minds, in the reality of the past, and in the external world are all held without inference and nobody calls them irrational. If the foundationalist framework permits those, the question is why it should exclude this one.
reformed.x: You did not infer that other people have minds. You have never seen anyone else's consciousness, and you are not irrational.
reformed.q: What must a Reformed epistemologist say to someone who declares belief in a random “Great Pumpkin” properly basic?
reformed.a: That proper basicality is not created by declaration. The belief needs the right kind of cognitive basis/conditions and must withstand relevant defeaters. The hard philosophical work is specifying those conditions without special pleading.

properly.w: The regress problem forces foundationalists to explain why stopping at some beliefs is not arbitrary. “Properly basic” names the status they need: a belief can be justified or warranted directly, without another belief serving as premise, while still being rationally assessable and defeasible.
properly.i: Beliefs that are rational without being derived from other beliefs. Everyone's framework contains some; the disagreement is entirely about which ones qualify and on what criterion.
properly.x: “I had breakfast this morning.” “Other people have minds.” “The world is more than five minutes old.”
properly.q: You remember eating breakfast and form “I ate breakfast” without constructing an argument. What would make that belief properly basic rather than arbitrary?
properly.a: An appropriate functioning memory state provides the non-inferential basis, and no defeating evidence is present. The belief is not premise-free because of preference; it is grounded in a source that supplies prima facie warrant directly.

flew.w: A belief can appear meaningful and evidentially supported while being protected from every possible counterexample. Flew applies the Popperian concern about immunizing stratagems to theology: if nothing can ever count against “God loves us,” what exactly is being asserted about the world?
flew.i: Flew took Popper's demarcation criterion and turned it on theology. His parable: two explorers find a clearing. One says a gardener tends it. No gardener is seen, so the gardener is invisible. Barriers detect nothing, so the gardener is intangible. Dogs do not scent him, so he is odourless. Flew's question: what began as an assertion has been qualified until nothing could count against it. At what point did it die “the death of a thousand qualifications”?
flew.x: Each qualification is individually reasonable. Cumulatively they empty the claim of content without anyone noticing the moment it happened.
flew.q: A claim survives every apparent counterexample by adding a new qualification after the fact. What is the precise Flew-style question to ask?
flew.a: “What, if anything, would you accept as counting against the claim?” If the honest answer is nothing, the issue is not that the claim has been disproved but that its empirical or discriminating content has been hollowed out.

fideism.w: Some religious commitments function less like scientific hypotheses and more like orienting commitments, forms of trust, or ways of life. Fideism exists to resist the demand that such commitments must first be validated by the same evidential procedures used for ordinary empirical claims.
fideism.i: Religious claims belong to a form of life with its own grammar. Applying an external evidential standard misunderstands what is being said, in the way that demanding proof of a hinge misunderstands what a hinge is.
fideism.q: A believer says the core commitment is not inferred from evidence but agrees that historical claims derived from it can be defeated by historical evidence. Is that necessarily inconsistent with fideism?
fideism.a: No. A moderate fideist can treat faith as non-evidentially grounded while allowing empirical claims and interpretations within the tradition to remain defeasible. The boundary, not total immunity, is the key question.
